The Deceased Wife Reborn in Heaven: Chen Fazang.
She was a native of Baqu in Wannian County, Yongzhou. By profession, she served as a kitchen attendant. In the eighteenth year of the Zhenguan era, she went on duty for the capital region (Luozhou).
Later, her wife passed away and she returned from her duty; she had been away from her original village for some ten days or more when she turned her head back [and saw a vision].
While traveling along the road, he encountered his deceased wife. His wife said, "I have already been dead for several days.

In a brief moment, Xiang suddenly saw eight or nine houses that resembled the dwellings of poor people; he sat in one of them, as the other buildings were few. At that time, his wife was called away and led off.
Following after her, Xiang saw his wife being impaled with an iron fork by a yak-headed hell-warden. Inside...

She was dug up from the cauldron, her flesh and bones scattered; she was impaled on a fork and returned to life. This occurred seven times in succession before she was finally released and came to see him.
Her appearance had become suddenly hideous, and she said to Zang, "I have become your junior wife. My predecessor died of her own accord; it was not harmed by me."
"Within your sleeve, my lord, you have five hundred coins. At home, there is an ox worth fifteen hundred. When you arrive home, please tell Grandmother:
'Please strive to copy the Lotus Sūtra for me; I shall then be able to escape this suffering. Take these words of mine and respectfully entreat Grandmother.
Once you have returned home, inform your mother. Sell the ox and obtain exactly fifteen hundred coins; then immediately summon a scribe and purchase paper."
Fearing that his wife might still be alive, Zang searched further for her whereabouts. Just as he began to knock on the door, he heard a voice from a neighboring house calling out from afar:
"Your new bride was reborn in heaven yesterday when she purchased paper. Upon hearing this, Zang’s joy and faith increased even more;

with the wealth he acquired, he regularly transcribed the *Lotus Sūtra*. For nineteen years, he made offerings and practiced the Way at Xingshan Temple, recounting these matters in detail to the various monks.
[This concludes] the tenth section, "Extolling and Praising.

Regarding Shenren Zhilu (The Spirit Man Pointing the Way), Yuan Zhitong was a native of Longcheng County. He recited the Lotus Sūtra; at the age of twenty, he was drafted into the military to serve in a campaign.

Tong traveled eight thousand *li* into the lands of the Eight Man tribes. He recited the scriptures without ceasing until he reached the southern border, where his army was defeated and many were wounded.
Tong was in a state of constant distress and alarm when suddenly five men appeared on horseback before him.

The last of them said to Tong, "Because you have cultivated the fruits of goodness and recited the sacred texts, we, the assembly of virtuous beings, shall protect you; we cannot allow harm to come to you. You must travel seven..."
About one *li* away, there was a stupa into which he could enter to hide; the barbarian then returned to his camp.

Furthermore, two monks appeared and said to Sengtong, "Because of the power of your recitation and study, we have just dispatched five people to protect you. You must remain diligent, for benevolent spirits will always assist and support you.
Having spoken, they ascended into the air and departed. From that time on, he passed through three battles without being struck by even a single blade of iron.
Tong returned after the Mian tribes were pacified. In the eighth year of the Zhenguan era, he passed away while ill. He saw messengers pursuing him to the presence of King Yama’s hall.
The King asked what virtuous deeds he had performed. Tong replied that he constantly observed the *Lotus Sūtra* fast, maintained the precepts, and performed rites of repentance.

Upon hearing this, the King joined his palms in praise and commanded that a golden bed and jade table be brought to the hall. He ordered rugs and cushions to be spread out and requested Tong to take the seat of honor and recite [the scripture].

He recited the scripture for one scroll and then stopped. The King said, "Your virtuous achievements are profound; you ought to further observe the hells so that you may know that retribution for sin and merit does not err.
Tong saw everything clearly and was struck with fear. He returned once more to the King's presence. The King said, "Since you have seen the hells, you should redouble your diligent cultivation.
For this reason, I now beg you to grant me long life. Tong regained consciousness and recounted the events as above. [End of excerpt]
*Collected Records of Auspicious Omens: Records of Manifested Responses*.
On the opening of lotuses in the twelfth month by Shi Fayong. His secular surname was Wei; he was a native of Xinting in Yanling, Danyang. He donned the black robes at a young age.
In secular life, he withdrew his shadow into the mountain forests to study the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Carrying his book-cases, he sought out teachers from no distance of a thousand li.
However, because he followed his own nature without constancy, he was not approved by his contemporaries.

Later, he returned to Youqi Temple on Mount Niutou in Danyang, where he built a separate small hut to diligently cultivate his former studies. Disciples from near and far flocked to him in great numbers; thus, before the cliffs and valleys, he established himself.
He lectured on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in its entirety. At that time, it was the height of winter, and thick frost covered the trees;
yet, at the site of the lecture, two stalks of golden lotuses suddenly sprang forth. The assembly was greatly amazed and marveled at this unprecedented occurrence.

Furthermore, there was a large deer that would regularly attend the lectures at the appointed times. His disciples were inspired to take the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as their primary practice. Later, [the master’s] whereabouts became unknown.
[This concludes the section on] "Those Who Met Their End. From the third volume of *Hongzan* (Extolling and Praising).

The Buddha’s prophecy concerning the lay devotee Lu Chun of the Heavenly Palace: he was a native of Wu who recited the *Lotus Sūtra* in its entirety, maintained a vegetarian diet, and observed lifelong fasting. [The year was] Daye...

In the fifth month of the second year, he fell gravely ill. After more than ten days had passed, for four days and four nights thereafter, he lay on his back gazing at the ceiling of his room, never once turning away.
The venerable teacher Ei, a close friend, came to visit him and asked, "What are you looking at?"
He replied, "The Buddha prophesied that I would be reborn in the Yāma Heaven. Now I see its celestial palaces, halls, temple buildings, groves, city gates, and the hosts of devas;
gazing upon them, I am so filled with joy that I am unaware of fatigue. Four days later, he passed away.
(From *Hongzan*, fascicle 7.)
Third Section: Chapter on Similes; Chapter on Resolute Belief; Chapter on the Parable of the Medicinal Herbs; Chapter on the Bestowal of Prophecy.
When the scrolls are heavy but the charges are light, the illness is cured and the lifespan is eternal.
The night was as bright as day; timely rain fell everywhere;
the incense in the burner perfumed itself without being heated; the blind man could see;
the weight of the scriptures outweighed the gravity of his crimes.
Liu Shi was a native of Pingkang Ward in Wannian County, Yongzhou. On the sixth day of the sixth month in the second year of the Yonglong era, he fell ill and died after two days.
Six days after his death, only the area of his heart remained warm; his family had already selected the date for the funeral and had not yet dared to shroud him.
At dawn on the seventh day, he suddenly revived and said: "At that time, I was led by a person into a great hall..."
The city’s palaces, towers, and pavilions were magnificent beyond compare. Upon seeing King Yama, he was told, "You must record in full the merits you performed while alive.
He replied that during his life he had read only two fascicles of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and possessed no other merit.

The King then summoned the dossier of his offenses and weighed him on the scale of karma; the two fascicles of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* proved heavier than the dossier of his sins. The King then examined the case file.
The oracle stated: "This person ought to live for ninety years. Consulting the registers, it was said that he should be released back home, whereby he was granted his life.
He subsequently received the precepts, abstaining from alcohol and meat, and commissioned a *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* written in golden characters to serve as a perpetual offering.
(From *Hongzan*, fascicle 9.)
At that time, his illness was cured and his life-span was forever secured by Huisi.
He was a native of Shixing. From his youth he pursued the Way and habitually recited the Lotus Sūtra more than three thousand times.
At the age of twenty-three, he suddenly fell ill with a seasonal epidemic. After several weeks had passed, he dreamed that someone led him to a certain place;
its walls and courtyards were red and white, exactly like an official residence. Upon entering the gate, he immediately saw a nobleman whose height was eight or nine feet.
He was wearing a crimson-purple robe and a black silk cap, and was said to be King Yama. The King asked the Master what meritorious deeds he had performed.
Zhi replied, "Since my youth, I have recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. The King said, "Then you may recite it.

Zhi immediately ascended a high seat, faced west, and recited the second fascicle of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Upon reaching the "Parable" chapter, [he recited]: "For example, there was an elder who had one..."
He then stayed at Dazhai. The King immediately rose and said, "Dharma Master, please return. He ordered two men to escort him back. Consequently, he regained his composure;
his illness was greatly relieved, and within a few days he had recovered. He was then able to recite the scriptures again. Furthermore, when he was fifty-five years old, his body fell ill once more.
Suddenly, he dreamed that he was standing atop the stupa of Guoxin Temple in Shixing. Someone pushed him down and said, "Beg [for mercy]."
His life, which had lasted for over eighty years, was thereby restored to health. He reached the age of eighty-two in the thirteenth year of the Daye era.
His final destination thereafter is unknown. This concludes the seventh entry from *Hongzan*.
There was an elderly man named Xin (his personal name is unknown), over eighty years of age, who lived in the southern corner of Zhengzhou City.
He regularly recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* with single-minded purity. For thirty years, he has recited the sutra every night; the night has become as bright as day.
One may use lamps and candles; however, if one sets aside the scripture scrolls, it returns to its usual darkness and objects can no longer be seen. (From *Hongzan*, fascicle 9).
At that time, rain fell everywhere.
Shi Huiyuan was born into the Pu clan; he was a native of Jingzhao. At the tender age of ten, he entered the monastic order under Dharma Master Jizang.
After receiving full ordination, he became widely learned and possessed great erudition. He lectured on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Later, he departed from human settlements to seek a dwelling in Langu Valley, where he enjoyed leisure and delighted in the Way. In the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era, while observing the summer retreat at the monastery, the weather happened to be exceptionally hot.
During a drought, he lectured on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to pray for sweet rain. People from near and far came to hear him; they gathered like clouds and followed like mist.

Every time, two elderly men arrived at the appointed hour. Since they were not acquaintances, Huiyuan noted their features and kept a record of them, contemplating their appearance and questioning himself about them, yet he did not voice his thoughts.
When the lecture reached the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter, a great rain fell in drenching abundance. The two elderly men who had appeared before did not come for three days.
Later, he arrived carrying his staff. Huiyuan was surprised and called out to question him. He then hesitated and replied, "I am a dragon, a disciple.
Recently, I was deeply moved by the Dharma Master’s exposition of the *Parable Chapter*, which opened the gate of skillful means. Thinking to repay this virtuous wisdom, I suddenly sent down rain.
However, as the season was not yet appropriate, I was struck with a cane by the Dragon King because I had precipitated the downpour prematurely. Thereupon, he suddenly vanished.
Huiyuan was naturally humble and courteous by disposition; even when encountering a śrāmaṇera, he would invariably dismount from his horse to inquire after him.

When someone asked him the reason for this, he replied: "The saffron robes are like the banner of the sages and immortals. Even a lion pays them respect; now that they have attained Perfect Enlightenment, how could I, a mere individual, dare not follow their example?
Huiyuan constantly recited the *Lotus Sūtra*, and it frequently manifested spiritual responses. At times, he would even cease adding oil [to his lamp].
The lamp wick burned brightly by itself for several days. (Recorded in *Hongzan* [Biographies of Eminent Monks], Section 3.
Regarding Shi Zhiyan: his secular surname was Zhu; he was a native of Wu Commandery. His grandfather was Xian, a Court Gentleman for the Secretariat under the Liang dynasty; his father was Min.
Chen served as a *fengchaoqing* (court-invited cleric). His mother was Lady Zhang. At the age of eight, he left the household life and became a disciple of Dharma Master Qu of Tongxuan Temple.

When Emperor Yang of the Sui Dynasty was still a prince in the provinces, he treated him with profound courtesy and esteem. Upon the Great Tang’s unification of the realm, he returned to Wuchuan Mountain Temple.

In addition to his lectures and recitations, he constantly performed the *Sūtra of the Lotus Flower* and the *Samantabhadra* repentances. He also recited the *Lotus Sūtra* more than three thousand times.

He lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra* more than thirty times. His spiritual resonance was in profound accord with the divine; auspicious omens were manifold. When the incense burner had not yet been heated at night, fragrant smoke would rise of its own accord;
when the evening libation was just finished, water would secretly overflow. He passed away in the eighth year of the Zhenguan era at the age of seventy-one.
This is recorded in the third fascicle of the *Hongzan*.
Gu Sou was blind yet could see the pure-faith layman Wang Fanxing.
Wang Fanxing was a native of Linyi in Langya. He lost both his eyes in his youth; his mother, out of compassionate concern for him, [nursed him].
He was orally instructed in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and by the age of thirteen, he had mastered the entire work.
He continued to recite and practice it day and night with single-minded devotion, reaching seventeen thousand recitations. Although he could not see, he did not require a guide when walking;

he naturally recognized pits and mounds. Furthermore, he was able to weave mats and screens, sew clothes, and write letters and notes more skillfully than those with sight. Everyone marveled at this, suspecting him to be extraordinary.
He attained realization. At the age of seventy-one, he passed away in the sixth year of the Kaihuang era. His remains were left in the wilderness; neither birds nor beasts dared to approach them.
Once his flesh had vanished, only his white bones remained. His tongue then emerged from his mouth, over a foot long and the color of a lotus flower.
His younger brother, Huiyi, placed it in a brick casket, and it did not decay for a long time.
The Fourth Section: The Cycle of Causes and Conditions; The Parable of the Phantom City.
Birds accustomed to hearing [the Dharma] were immediately liberated from their karmic bodies; bhikṣus reciting [the sūtra] from memory were instantly freed from the calamity of ghosts.
Thus, the master and disciple of a former life were moved to realization, and fathers and sons across two lifetimes were reunited.
Birds, having long been accustomed to hearing [the Dharma], were able to cast off their karmic bodies.
During the Eastern Jin dynasty, there was a monk named Fazhi who built a hermitage on Mount Yuhang. He recited the Lotus Sūtra morning and evening without ceasing.

A pheasant had built its nest beside the hermitage. Every time it heard the sound of reciting sutras, it would fly and gather at the side of the seat, appearing as if standing in attendance to listen and receive instruction.
This continued for seven years. One day, the bird became emaciated and haggard. The Master stroked it and said, "Though you belong to the feathered race, you have been able to listen to the sutras;
if you were to cast off this karmic body, you would surely be reborn in the human realm. The next morning, the bird suddenly died. He then buried it immediately.
When it was night, he dozed off and dreamed that a young boy bowed twice before him and said, "I am a pheasant.

Because I listened to you, Master, reciting the sutras, I have now been reborn as a male child in the household of the Wang family in front of this mountain. There is still a pheasant feather in my right armpit for you to verify.
The next morning, the monk went to the Wang family’s home and questioned them; it was indeed so. One day, when the Wang family prepared a vegetarian feast, Zhi Fang followed behind the door. This—
The son suddenly exclaimed, "My Master has come! The entire assembly marveled at this. He brought it to show Zhì, who stroked it and said, "This is indeed my pheasant chick.
He then removed his robe and examined its armpits; there were indeed three feathers of a pheasant.
When he reached the age of seven, his parents permitted him to leave the household life. At the appropriate time, he entered the mountains and received the tonsure at sixteen;
because there was wool on his armpits, he was named Tanyi. He was granted a copy of the Lotus Sūtra without missing a single character.

Having become a monk, he traveled in various directions seeking the Way and attained realization of the essential vehicle (zongcheng). He acquired great eloquence and traveled east to Kuaiji, eventually arriving at Qinwang Mountain.
He then cleared away stones and cut down brambles to establish a hermitage for his mountain retreat. He devoted himself exclusively to reciting the *Lotus Sūtra* for nearly ten years.
One day, as the sun was setting, a woman appeared before the Master, dressed in colorful garments and carrying a bamboo basket containing a white pig and two large garlic bulbs.
She stood before him and said with tears: "I am the daughter of such-and-such a family from the foot of this mountain; I have come into the mountains to gather [herbs]."
Wei encountered a fierce tiger on the road and fled to this place. The sun had already set; the trees and grasses cast deep shadows, and jackals and wolves roamed about.
With no means of returning home, she asked, "May I venture to entrust myself to you for one night? Would that be permissible? The Master, citing grounds of suspicion, firmly refused her request.

The woman shed tears like rain and wailed piteously. Having no other choice, the Master yielded a straw mat to her, whereupon she immediately covered her head and recited the sutras until the third watch.
She cried out again as her illness flared up, claiming she had abdominal pain. Master Yi examined her; the master administered medicine to her, but the woman’s pain grew even more severe.
She could not stop crying out and said, "If you would only press and massage my navel and abdomen for me, I might find some slight relief;
otherwise, I shall die. The Buddha-dharma takes compassion and skillful means as its foundation. Master, how can you bear to sit idly by and not help?"
She reached out her hand and asked for help. The Master said, "I am a monk who has received the Great Precepts. To touch a woman’s body—what kind of principle is this?

Because her entreaty was so earnest, he immediately wrapped the head of his iron staff in a cloth and used it from a distance to rub and press her. After a short while, he announced, "It is already healed.
The next morning, the woman emerged at the edge of the courtyard; her colorful garments transformed into auspicious clouds, the pig changed into a white elephant, and the garlic transformed.
The Twin Lotuses: A woman with feet treading upon lotuses, striding across an elephant and riding upon clouds, said to him, "I am the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.
Since you shall soon return to my assembly, I have come specifically to test you and observe the state of your mind; it is like the moon in water, incapable of being defiled.
Having spoken, she vanished into the distance. At that moment, flowers rained down from the heavens, and the earth trembled everywhere.
Movement. On this day, the Governor, Lord Meng Yi, was just rising from his morning sleep when he suddenly beheld auspicious clouds billowing in the south, their radiance piercing the courtyard.
Beneath the clouds, there was the faint sound of metal, stone, silk, and bamboo instruments. Upon inquiry, he learned of Master Puxian’s passing into transformation.
He then reported the Master’s spiritual conduct to the imperial court, whereupon an edict was issued to establish a monastery, with the plaque inscribed as follows:
Regarding the *Lotus Sūtra*: it was during the thirteenth year of the Yixi era of Emperor An of the Jin dynasty.
According to the *Chuxian yinglu* and the inscription on the stele of Fahua Temple, a bhikṣu recited the sūtra from memory and thereby escaped the calamity of a ghostly affliction.
Formerly, at a mountain monastery in a foreign land, there was a young bhikṣu who recited the Lotus Sūtra daily.
Once, while walking in meditation outside the temple, he encountered a rākṣasī demoness who transformed herself into a woman of exquisite beauty. She came to disturb the bhikṣu;

infatuated by her, he subsequently consorted with her. Afterward, his spirit became dazed and vacant, and he lost all awareness. The demoness carried him off on her back and flew through the air. When she wished—

He returned to his original place, intending to devour him. During the first watch of the night, as he was passing over a monastery, the bhikṣu who was above the ghost heard the sound of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* being recited within the monastery. Consequently, he became slightly alert and remembered what he himself had studied.
He then recited it from memory in his mind. The ghost immediately felt heavy; gradually drawing closer to the ground, it was finally unable to support its weight and abandoned him, departing.
After a short while, the bhikṣu regained consciousness. Hearing the sound of a bell, he followed the sound to the temple, knocked on the door, and requested entry.

He recounted the beginning and end of the matter in detail. However, when calculated, he had already traveled more than two thousand li from his hometown. The monks said, "This man has committed a grave offense."

They could not dwell together. An elder remarked, "This is a delusion caused by a spirit; it is not one's own mind. Once he was freed from the affliction, the elder said, "The power of the present sutra is evident;
you may remain at the temple to perform repentance. Later, when you encounter a person of faith from that region, you may then depart.
(Recorded in *Hongzan*, fascicle 6.)
Regarding Shi Tandi, who was inspired by his realization of his former life as a teacher and disciple: His ancestors were from Kangju. Later, they moved to Wuxing.

While his mother, Lady Huang, was sleeping during the day, she dreamed that a monk called out to her as "Mother," entrusting her with a fly-whisk (*chǔwěi*) and an iron-inlaid book-press. After Huang had fallen asleep...
Upon waking, he saw that both objects were still there. His mother was secretly surprised by this, and consequently became pregnant and gave birth to Sengdi.
When Sengdi was five years old, his mother played with him using a fly-whisk and other items. Sengdi said, "These were gifts from the King of Qin. His mother asked, "Where did you put them?"
He replied, "I do not remember. When he reached the age of ten, he left home to become a monk. His learning did not derive from a teacher; his awakening arose spontaneously from Heaven.
Later, while following his father to Fandeng, he encountered the monk Dao Ren [Qie-Da-Shi] of Guanzhong. Suddenly, he called out, "Qie! Dao Ren asked, "Child, why do you call an elder by name?
Da Di replied, "The Venerable A-shang was originally Da Di as a śrāmaṇera; you once served the community of monks..."
While gathering vegetables, he was wounded by a wild boar; he did not even realize it until he involuntarily let out a cry. Why do you now forget this?
Furthermore, the monk Sengqie had been a disciple of Master Hongjue. While gathering vegetables for the monks, he was wounded by a wild boar, yet Sengqie initially had no recollection of this.
He then went to see Daodi’s father, who recounted the full details of Daoshi’s origins and presented him with the letter, the seal, the whisk, and other items.
Xie Daoshi then realized and wept, saying, "This is none other than my late master, Dharma Master Hongjue.

When that master was lecturing on the *Lotus Sūtra* for Yao Chang, the ruler of the Qin, I served as the assistant lecturer (*dujiang*). Yao Chang presented two items to the master, which have now come to be here.
Calculating back from the time of Master Hongjue’s passing, it was precisely the day he entrusted these items to me. Furthermore, I recall the incident of gathering wild vegetables."

My grief and lamentation increase all the more. He traveled extensively to study both internal and external teachings; he could memorize them upon merely glancing at them. He lectured on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* fifteen times each.
He passed away at the end of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty. Fei Changfang said: "The Dharma Master Hongjue’s disciple was Sengqi.
Both master and disciple were renowned for their mastery of the Way throughout the two Qin regions. Their personal effects, including the three robes, were likewise beyond measure. Only—"

He kept his writing-brush and fly-whisk (zhǔwěi) with great care, cherishing them in his breast. When he was about to transfer consciousness and undergo rebirth, these two items were thus able to accompany him.
This is from the second version of the *Hongzan* [Biographies of Eminent Monks], compiled from the *Gaoseng zhuan*.

In the Silla kingdom, there was a man named General Kim Geu-i, who had sons by two wives from different generations. He fathered a son who left home to become a monk at a young age and delighted in reading the Lotus Sūtra.
When he reached the second fascicle, he mistakenly burned one character. At the age of eighteen, he suddenly passed away. He was reborn in another region into the family of Jin Guoyi.

Having again entered the monastic order, he began to study and recite the *Lotus Sūtra* in its entirety; however, whenever he reached the second fascicle, he would forget each character as soon as it was questioned.
In a dream, someone said to him: "The junior monk’s previous life was in such-and-such a village, in the family of such-and-such a Jin Guoyi..."
Yi was born into that family and also attained ordination. During his previous life, while reciting the *Lotus Sūtra*, he had mistakenly burned one character;
for this reason, in his present life, he forgets it as soon as he learns it. That old manuscript of the scripture still exists there.

Following a dream, this junior monk sought out that place and indeed found the family. He inquired about lodging and asked after his parents from his previous life, who were still faintly recognizable.
Shi searched through old scriptures and discovered that the second character was indeed "burn" (shāo). The young disciple and his former parents were overcome with a mixture of grief and joy;

the two families subsequently became close friends, regarding one another as no different from their own kin. They immediately reported this to the local prefectures and counties, which submitted the matter to the throne.
The news spread throughout the nation in song. This occurred during the Zhenguan era. Excerpted from *Hongzan* (Extensive Praise), fascicle nine.
Fifth Section: The Chapter on the Prophecy for the Five Hundred Disciples; The Chapter on Bestowing Prophecies upon Those in Training and Those Beyond Training;
The Partridge Suddenly Transforms Its Body; King Yama Raises His Hand and Snap His Fingers.
Melted butter filled the vessels and the military guards filled the courtyard;
spirits and deities alerted him as he went to board his boat, while the Lord of Heaven withdrew the scriptures to enter the treasury.
Suddenly, a wild pheasant turned its body.
The Master’s name was Daosheng. He lived in seclusion at Huqiu Temple, where a stone lecture platform remains to this day.

For a time he resided at Bantang, where he recited the Lotus Sūtra. Suddenly, a pheasant would regularly come to listen. One day it was not seen, and the Master missed it. That night it appeared in a dream and said:
"Because I listened to your recitation of the sūtra, I have been able to change my karmic retribution. I am now the son of a certain family."
He waited for several years before returning to serve him. When the Master questioned him, it was indeed so.
Not long after he had left home, the boy passed away at the age of seven and was buried in the forest. One night, he suddenly emitted a light that shone brilliantly across the ponds and ravines.
The villagers found this strange. When they opened [the tomb] to look, they discovered a tongue from which a living blue lotus had grown.
Consequently, a stūpa was erected there, and later it was developed into a temple, which is the present-day Bantang Temple. (From *Chuxian yinglu*, Part 1)
King Yama raised his eyebrows and snapped his fingers to release Shi Huidu.
Huidu was a native of Wuxing who maintained a vegetarian diet and observed the perpetual fast. He regularly recited the Lotus Sūtra; suddenly he fell ill and died a violent death.

On the fifth day, he returned to life. He himself recounted that he had seen King Yama; the king wore the *yuanyou* crown and robes with sashes like those of a contemporary monarch, and his attendants were likewise arrayed.

At first, the king’s countenance was mild and refined, and he presided over the adjudication of offenses. Suddenly, he became greatly enraged; his beard and face contorted in a strange manner. He asked, "What karma do you have?
He replied, "I recite the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. The king stood up straight, snapped his fingers, and summoned [the monk] forth.
He was invited to sit upon a golden couch and requested to recite the scripture once through to its conclusion. The King said, "This merit is inconceivable;
by the power of this sutra, the Dharma Master’s lifespan shall be sustained and extended for another two cycles. Subsequently, he indeed lived for twenty-four years longer.
He passed away during the Yuanjia era of Emperor Wen of the Chen dynasty at the age of over seventy. [Recorded] from the *Hongzan*.
Sixth: Rong Su-man Qi Shi Zhi-zang (Melted Butter-Filled Vessel Śrī-jñānagarbha).
A native of Xiazhou, he left home to become a monk at an early age and resided at Daxingshan Temple. He regularly recited the Lotus Sūtra.
He limited the recitation of the sutra to one thousand repetitions. Consequently, his heart was injured and he vomited blood for several days. A monk from the temple named Jì Mù told Zhāng:
"I have heard that for an injury to the heart, one should mix urine with flour to make a gruel and drink it; then one will recover.

Zhāng replied, "I have vowed not to defile the sutra with impure substances within these one thousand repetitions. Although this may serve as medicine, it ultimately contradicts my original resolve. Thereupon, he sprinkled [water]...
He swept the courtyard and prepared an altar, placing the scriptures upon it. He burned incense, circumambulated, and prostrated with sincere devotion.
That night, as if in a dream, he saw a Brahman monk who mixed water with flour to make a paste and gave it to Xuanzang to drink.

Before Xuanzang had finished half the draught, he suddenly awoke; his mental and physical strength was doubled compared to usual, and he returned to following his former regimen. This occurred in the summer of the ninth year of the Zhenguan era.
The monk Shi Fa-shi of the province heard that Guṇabhadra was reciting the sutras and offered three jin of ghee as an offering. Guṇabhadra placed it in a single vessel;
on the first day, he took a portion about the size of a peach from the center using a copper spoon. On the next day, when he took more, he saw that the old spot was filled with solidified ghee.
From summer until autumn, he took portions as before, and Guṇabhadra rejoiced in his heart, for the first time realizing the essence of the *Tattvasaṃgraha*.
Ghee emerged spontaneously from within it. In the eighth month, he divided this aged ghee and gave it to the Chan Master Lingxiang of the same monastery, explaining the matter to him.
Furthermore, he frequently smelled extraordinary fragrances and heard the sound of finger-snapping; on several occasions, he was summoned by a person from the netherworld to rise.
He recited [the scriptures] more than ten thousand times in total throughout his life. In the third year of the Yifeng era, at the age of eighty-eight, he passed away at Jingying Temple.
However, because his observance of the precepts was slightly deficient, he did not attain profound awakening; those who understood him lamented this.
(From *Hongzan*, fascicle 8.)

Bingwei Yingting Shi Sengying left home to become a monk in his youth and resided at Yongqi Temple in Jiangyang. He recited the Lotus Sūtra, continuing his study and recitation without ceasing even until old age.
He shared a room with a certain Dharma Master who was constantly annoyed by the high volume of his recitation, feeling it was a disturbance.

He ceased his reading and requested Master Xuan to admonish him. That night, at the beginning of the first watch, the moon was bright. As the monk Sengying recited the sutras as usual, Master Xuan intended to go and advise him to stop.

Upon opening the door and looking out, he saw several thousand people before Sengying’s room, clad in armor and holding bows and weapons, kneeling with palms joined in the foreign fashion to listen to the recitation of the sutras. Master Xuan immediately withdrew and returned to his own quarters. The next morning...
Ribei recounted to this Dharma Master what he had seen during the previous night, and they went together to repent for their sins of resentment and hatred.
Ying, who usually traveled with the sound of armored troops heard before and behind him, passed away at the temple during the Kaihuang era.
Excerpted from *Hongzan* (Extolling and Praising), Volume Seven.
A divine being alerted him while he was sleeping and approached his boat, releasing a precious jade pendant.

This was Zhang Xiaoxiu’s younger brother; he had left the household life to dwell at Kuangshan Temple and recited the *Lotus Sūtra* with great fluency and mastery, yet he was unable to properly restrain his body and speech.
Prince Shaoling of the Liang dynasty took offense at this and secretly dispatched two men during the night to...

Wang Jue was going to kill him. At that time, Jue was lying on his bed resting when he suddenly dreamed that four men came before the bed and shook Jue’s hand, saying, "The Prince of Shaoling has sent people to kill you;
how can you sleep so peacefully? Jue woke up in alarm and immediately rose.
He opened the door toward the rear, yet he still perceived the sound of someone entering through the front door; his heart grew increasingly terrified.
He went out to the back of the room, where there was a pond that had never before been entered by him, its depth unknown.

In a state of dazed confusion, he suddenly saw a boat with two men leaning on their poles waiting for him. Jue then boarded the boat and reached the opposite shore, where he immediately saw Shao-ling.

The two men sent by the king had already reached the edge of the pond, but they could only take water and were unable to cross over. Thereafter, [the Master] devoted himself to reading and reciting the scriptures with great diligence;
he became skilled at interpreting the sutras and was emulated by others. People of the time called him "Lu Shan Sha Qi" (Lushan the Sutra-Cutter), which refers to this very person.
Chapter Six: On the Propagation and Praise [of the Dharma].
The Heavenly Emperor Invited the Sūtras into the Tripiṭaka. Regarding the Mistress of the House, Jeongha:
she was the illegitimate daughter of King Kangjong and the wife of the powerful minister, Duke Pin-gang. She possessed great influence.
The iceberg will not last long; sighing over this ephemeral life as a burning house where there is no peace, he contemplated practicing the essential path of liberation.

Fortunate to have heard of the Perfect and Wondrous [Dharma], he first established the White Lotus Society. Together with those sharing his vows, he brought it to completion, providing diligent external protection. Furthermore, he fashioned a statue of the Tathāgata Amitāyus.
It was enshrined in the main hall. Furthermore, he vowed to produce the *Lotus Sūtra* in golden characters, ensuring that every detail of its adornment was complete without exception.
He entrusted it to Enmyō, who requested the mountain recluse Ichinyo to transcribe it. Later, in a dream, a divine being descended from the sky and said:
"The *Lotus Sūtra* in golden characters you have transcribed has already been placed in the second storey of the Āḷavi treasury in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven."
From the *Chūhai Tōden Kōroku* (Record of the Propagation Transmitted from the East).
Section Six: Chapter on the Dharma Master; Chapter on Seeing the Jeweled Stupa;
"Ghosts Cannot Harm; The Tongue Cannot Be Plowed."
The debtors returned the principal, the Immortal Elder specially invited him to the first rank,
he snapped his fingers in mid-air, incense arose upon his seat,
and ghosts could not harm him.
In the twenty-eighth year of the Shaoxing era, Li Yu, a military officer of Wuweijun, was escorting the new Prefectural Governor to the west of the city.
After traveling some ten li, he suddenly saw about a hundred people emerge from the roadside; they all appeared to be children of three or five years of age.
They rushed forward shouting and surrounded him to attack. At first, Li was not afraid and engaged them in combat; every time he raised his fist, [he struck].
About ten men fell to the ground; as soon as they fell, they rose again, and having dispersed, they closed ranks once more.

This occurred four times in succession. Some leaped up to mount his shoulders to seize his headcloth and loosen his hair. Li Yi fled in desperation, unable to escape; he struck back as he pressed forward.
Suddenly, an old man appeared, wearing a coarse robe and straw sandals, his origin unknown. He shouted with a stern voice, "This official always carries [it]..."
"If this *Lotus Sūtra* harms others, would it not bring trouble upon me? He rebuked them and ordered them to withdraw; the ghosts then dispersed, and the old man likewise vanished.
The old man suspected that the local tutelary deity had appeared. This is recorded in the *Yijianzhi*; for details, see the *Xianyingshu*.
During the Longshuo era, Gao Wenchang of the capital was reciting the Lotus Sūtra. One day, while riding out through Shunyi Gate on horseback, he suddenly saw two riders pursuing and seizing him.
When questioned, they said, "We have been sent by King Yama to pursue you. Wen—
Terrified and fleeing in all directions, none could escape; they were immediately dragged down from their horses, and their hair was pulled out as if being cut by a blade.
Their families carried them back home, and when night fell, he revived and said: "The King of Yama asked me why I had stolen the monks' confections and why I had spoken ill of the Triple Gem.
Consequently, I was made to confess my crimes according to the law and dared not utter a word in defense. The King passed judgment on my crime of stealing the fruit."

He was made to swallow four hundred and fifty iron pellets, which he received over the course of four years. His transgressions were recounted, and his tongue was made to plow the ground; consequently, he was released and subsequently revived.
After a short while, he again lost consciousness, and his mouth appeared as if it were swallowing something. His entire body broke out in red blisters, bearing the marks of intense suffering.
After another day had passed, he regained his senses and said: "I remained in hell for four days until the swallowing of the pellets was finished. The suffering..."

The poison was such that it could not be described; he was about to pull out his tongue and plow with it, but though he pulled, it would not come out. Upon investigation, it was found that he had regularly recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and thus his tongue could not be extracted.
He was subsequently released and restored to life. It is said that he is currently at Huadu Temple, in the presence of Master Yuánmǎn, where he listens to the Dharma and performs repentance.
This is excerpted from the *Nanshan Sānrǎo Gǎntōng Lù* (Records of Miraculous Responses to the Three Jewels of the Southern Mountains); details may be found in the *Hóng*.
The Ninth Scroll of the *Zàn* (Praise) explains the biography of Fayan and the *Xiànyìnglù* (Record of Manifestations and Responses).
The messenger returned with the principal sum;
Yan Gong, whose courtesy name was Jinli, was originally a native of Quanzhou. His family was wealthy, yet he had no brothers. His parents...

Sengcong was filial and respectful, and his words were never at variance with his actions. At the beginning of the Dajian era of the Chen dynasty, Sengcong requested permission from his parents, wishing to obtain fifty thousand coins to go to Yangzhou to purchase goods.
His parents granted his request. Sengcong boarded a boat, loaded it with the money, and traveled downstream.

When he was several tens of *li* away from Yangzhou, he encountered a boat on the river carrying soft-shelled turtles (the *Shuowen* defines a *yuan* as a large turtle) that was about to be taken to the market for sale. Sengcong questioned him.

Knowing the reason for this, he thought that the tortoises were about to die and requested to redeem them. The owner of the tortoises said, "My tortoises have large heads; one thousand coins per head is required.
Zeng asked how many heads there were. He replied, "There are fifty. Zeng said, "I have fifty thousand coins; I wish to redeem them with these.
The owner was pleased, took the money, handed over the tortoises, and departed. Zeng released all the tortoises into the river.
The empty boat set sail for Yangzhou. Its master, Gong, traveled another ten-odd *li* when the boat sank and he died.
That evening, as dusk fell, fifty guests dressed in black came to Gong’s home to stay overnight. They gave fifty thousand coins to Gong’s parents, saying, "Your son is in Yangzhou;
we have sent these coins back for him. We hope you will accept them according to their value. Gong’s father...
The mother was startled and alarmed, suspecting that Gong had died. The guest said, "The boy is well; he simply did not require money, so I sent it back with me.
Gong’s father accepted it, noting that it was the original capital, yet it was all damp from the water. He kept the guest and prepared a meal for him. The guest took his leave the following morning.
More than a month later, Gong returned home. His parents were overjoyed. Shortly thereafter, they asked about the source of the money sent with the guest, and Gong spoke.

He had none. When his parents described the appearance of the guest and the date and month when the money was attached—precisely the day the tortoises were ransomed—they realized that all fifty guests were the tortoises they had redeemed.
Father and son were struck with wonder and moved their residence to Yangzhou, where they devoted themselves exclusively to meritorious deeds.

He constantly read the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. Once, while reading, he reached the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Jeweled Stupa" (*Bao ta pin*). He set aside the scripture and sighed, saying, "The Jeweled..."
Within the stupa were two Tathāgatas, and the number of their manifested bodies was not small. "Why am I now unable to move them to appear before me?
he lamented for a long time. At night, he suddenly dreamed of a Hu monk who said to him: "If you recite this sutra..."
"If one wishes to see the Buddhas, one should explain, transcribe, circulate, and make offerings [to the scriptures];
then this aspiration may be fulfilled. Out of deep reverence for these words, he resolved to produce one hundred copies of the sutras. Before he had completed this task, he suddenly fell gravely ill.

He then made a renewed vow to increase the production to one thousand copies. Once his illness had healed, he immediately constructed a scripture hall within his residence; as for the paper and brushes, they were necessarily...
His mind was pure, and he never practiced deception. He managed his affairs as they arose and constantly maintained a dozen or so students, providing for them according to the Dharma.
Gong personally supervised their needs, never complaining of fatigue even when exhausted. Once, someone came to borrow ten thousand coins for sutras; Gong had no choice but to give them to him.
Having received the money, the man’s boat suddenly capsized in midstream. The money was lost, but the man survived. On that very day...

Senggong entered the storehouse and saw that the original coins were all damp; he found this quite strange. Later, when he saw those who had borrowed them, he learned they had been submerged in water.
One day, there suddenly appeared a strange monk about eighty years old, who said he had come from the kingdom of Kucha and was now heading for Mount Luofu.
Hearing that Senggong was producing scriptures, he wished to request one copy. Senggong bestowed the scripture upon him, and the monk presented him with a jar of gold, which weighed—
"Forty liang. I wish to assist in the creation of this scripture. Having said this, he withdrew and no one knew where he went.
Furthermore, Hou Zhi came from Poyang to Gongting. There, someone led him into a temple, where he saw a divine being sitting with a sword resting on his knee.
The being asked Zhi, "Do you still recognize Yan Gong, who created the *Lotus Sūtra* in Yangzhou? I wish to entrust ten thousand coins to him for the merit of this work."
Having spoken, the deity vanished. The next day, Hui-zhi arrived at Dangtu. Suddenly, a man came to seek him out;

he left ten thousand coins behind, pressing him to accept them before departing. Hui-zhi reflected on this and knew they were divine coins. As soon as he reached Yangzhou, he gave the money to Seng-gong.
Gong and Zhi became even more resolute, and they produced three thousand copies [of the scripture]. Furthermore, there was a fisherman who one night...
He saw flames rising one after another floating upon the river. He steered his boat toward them, and they were found to be a single case of scriptures.

These were the very ones that Yan Gong had produced. Later, he made this vow: "There shall not be a single character that has not passed before my eyes, nor a single character that has not been applied with my whole heart.
Indeed, the number of scriptures produced by Yan Gong was so vast that his descendants continued the tradition of his craft; he was known in the world as Yan Fahua. (Sui Dynasty)
During the reign of Emperor Ji, bandits were rampant. When they reached Jiangdu, the inhabitants all made a mutual agreement not to enter the district of Yan Fahua.
Because of this, the district was spared from destruction. He transcribed over two thousand five hundred fascicles in total.
This account originally appears in the *Lingshui ji* and the *Gantong lu*, with further details found in the tenth fascicle of the *Hongzan* and the *Xianying lu*.
The Immortal Elder specifically requested this first chapter.

Formerly, there was a Dharma Master who constantly recited the Lotus Sūtra. One day, while traveling on a mountain path, he encountered a servant who invited him into a small vegetarian feast within the mountains.
Upon reaching the gate, an elderly man of extraordinary appearance and demeanor came out to bow to him.
He was invited inside, where a high seat was prepared for him. The old man requested, "I wish to hear the 'Precious Stūpa' chapter. The Master ascended the seat and recited it once.
The old man presented him with a peach and a piece of gold leaf as a gift, then ordered a servant to escort him out.
As the Master reached the mouth of the valley, he asked the servant, "Who is that old man? The servant wrote the character for "Sūn" (孫) on the Master's palm with his finger.
His name was Simiao. His servant subsequently vanished. The Master ate peaches and did not die; he sold gold and became suddenly wealthy. [This account] appears in the *Yinglu*.
From the sky, there was the sound of a finger-snap.

The monk Daoyi of Qiling Monastery in Yangzhou constantly recited this sutra. Every time he reached the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Jeweled Stupa," he would snap his fingers several dozen times in the air.
From that time forward, his diligent recitation was twice as constant as before.
Sengzuo Shengxiang was a native of Wannian in Yongzhou. He recited the Lotus Sūtra and was also skilled in expounding its principles, having lectured upon it more than ten times.
Once, while he was reciting the sūtra beneath the eaves of his dwelling, a white pheasant suddenly appeared and submitted itself calmly at his side; he reached out his hand and took hold of it.
At first, there was no alarm or disturbance; things appeared and disappeared according to their forms. Sometimes charcoal embers emerged spontaneously from within the incense burner;

sometimes strange fragrances frequently wafted from between the mats behind the bed. Furthermore, a gilded bronze shrine containing an image arrived without warning atop a wooden beam behind the room.
A pair of blue magpies stood in attendance on either side, their forms perfectly composed; suddenly, the birds flew away.

Again, while sitting in meditation during the stillness of midnight, he suddenly saw, as if in a dream, a jeweled stupa in the northwest heavens, vast, lofty, and magnificently adorned, appearing boundless to the eye.
Furthermore, from within the Seven Stars in the northeast, the seven Buddhas emerged from the constellations, their golden countenances serene and pure, radiating a brilliant light.
Suddenly, he appeared in a brilliant blaze; they wept and rejoiced together as they performed prostrations and offered praises. Within a brief moment, he vanished instantly.
He had recited [the name] over four thousand times in total. As his end approached, he instructed his disciples to chant the name of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
Suddenly he himself said, "The Bodhisattva Samantabhadra has come," and passed away on his right side at the age of seventy-four.
This concludes the eighth volume of the *Hongzan* (Extensive Praise), section seven: the Chapter on Devadatta and the Chapter on Encouraging the Retention [of the Sūtra].
The body entrusted to a lotus-womb; the name inscribed upon a flower-seat; the holy monk reciting the teachings; the ocean deity requesting to hear [the Dharma];
the pigeon receiving a human body; the ghost liberated from its latrine-retribution;
the body entrusted to a lotus-womb.
Wang Yan, courtesy name Gongyuan, was a native of Linyi in Langya. His grandfather, Wang Fen, served as the Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs.

Yan himself held office as a Gentleman Attendant at the Gate and later became the Governor of Xin’an. He devoted his heart entirely to the Buddhist Way, never flagging in his practice from morning until night.

For many years he had been reciting the *Lotus Sūtra*. His younger brother, Gu, also maintained a vegetarian diet and recited the *Lotus Sūtra*. After Yan passed away, he appeared in a dream to Gu and said: [text continues].
"I have been born in the Western Land of the Buddha Amitāyus, within an iron-leafed lotus flower.
It will be five hundred years before I emerge from the womb to see the Buddha. Because I recited the Lotus Sūtra with such profound sincerity, I have attained birth in the West;

yet because I was foolish and full of doubt, I have undergone this womb-birth. I inform you of this merely to let you know. You must not be indolent in your recitation of the sūtras. Thereupon, they parted.
[End of section]. From the sixth volume of *Hongzan* (Extolling and Praising):

The monk Kējū of Kaigen-ji Temple in Mingzhou, whose name was inscribed upon a flower-seat [as a bodhisattva], constantly recited the *Lotus Sūtra*. He was commonly known as "Jū Hoke" (Jū of the Lotus). Throughout his life...

He recited [the scriptures] in reverse order, maintaining his practice for the benefit of others and adorning the Pure Land. In the eighth year of the Yuanyou era, he passed away while sitting upright and free from illness.

After three days, he revived and said, "I have already traveled spiritually to the Pure Land. The features of that land are identical to the adornments described in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (Sixteen Contemplations).
In the ponds of the seven treasures, every lotus pedestal bears the surname of one who is to be reborn there."
The names were: one purple-golden platform marked with "Xun Fahua of Guangjiao Monastery, Chengdu Prefecture, Great Song;
already born therein. Another golden platform marked "Twelfth Young Master Sun of Mingzhou. Another golden platform marked "Jiu Fahua of Mingzhou.
Another silver platform marked "Madam Xu of Mingzhou. Having finished speaking, she sat upright and passed away. Later, [the platforms appeared].

Five years later, the Daoist nun Xu indeed passed away while sitting in meditation. At the time of her death, a wondrous fragrance was perceived filling the room. Twelve years later, Sun Shierlang also passed away;

at that time, the sound of celestial music was heard. These successive auspicious signs originally appear in the *Longshu Jingtuwen* (Pure Land Texts of Longshu), as seen in detail in the *Xianyueling* (Records of Manifest Responses).

The Venerable Monk Jiao was a native of Bingzhou during the Sui dynasty named Gao Shoujie. His family had followed the faith for generations, yet Shoujie was particularly devoted and meticulous in his practice.
When he was sixteen or seventeen years old, while traveling to the capital of Dai, he encountered a śramaṇa on the road who appeared to be about sixty years old and called himself Haiyun.
He conversed with him and asked, "My son, can you recite the sutras? He replied, "It is indeed my sincere heart's desire. Yun then took him toward Mount Wutai.
Upon reaching a certain place, they saw three thatched huts, just large enough to accommodate their bodies; there they stayed.
Yun taught him to recite the *Lotus Sūtra* and went out to beg for food and clothing to provide for him. From time to time, he saw foreign monks coming there and [interacting] with him.
The Master spoke and laughed all day long. After the envoy had departed, Yun would repeatedly ask him, "Do you recognize that foreign monk from before? He replied, "I do not recognize him.
Yun, as if joking, said, "He is Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva. Although the envoy received this notice several times, he did not yet understand its significance.
Later, Yun suddenly sent the envoy down the mountain to fetch some items, and further instructed him, saying, "As for women, they are the source of manifold evils..."
The root of this is to ruin the path to Bodhi and destroy the city of Nirvana. As you head toward the human realm, you ought to be deeply cautious.

Jie respectfully accepted the instruction. On the way down the mountain, he saw a woman about fourteen or fifteen years old, whose clothing was bright and elegant, and whose compassionate countenance was refined and beautiful.
She rode a white horse directly up to him and said to Jie, "I am suffering from an urgent ailment and require..."
"You must dismount. The horse was prone to leaping about; though he tried to restrain it, he could not control it. He pleaded, "I hope you will assist me in supporting this humble life.
Sengjie then recalled his master’s words and ultimately did not look back. The woman pursued him for several li, her words earnest and piteous, yet Sengjie remained firm in his resolve as before.
Suddenly, she lost sight of him. Having returned to his original location, he related the events in detail. His master said, "You are truly a man of measure."
Truly so! Nevertheless, this was Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva; at that time, he had not yet attained awakening and still regarded it as mere playful speech.

Thus, he spent three full years reciting this sutra until he had thoroughly mastered the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in its entirety. Later, hearing that people were being ordained in Chang’an, his heart longed for the tonsure.
Through skillful means morning and evening, he consulted his master about his desire to depart. His master said, "You have mastered the recitation..."
"The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*—the seeds of the Mahāyāna have now already matured. If you must go, you should consult a good teacher;
this parting makes it difficult for us to meet again. Within the capital, you may rely upon Master Wo Lun at the Chan Meditation Hall.
Wait until the next term to enter the capital and seek ordination. His request was not granted, so he went to Lun’s place. Lun asked, "Where have you come from?"
He replied, "I have come from Mount Wutai. A monk there sent me to you to be your disciple. Yun-lun asked, "What is that monk's name? He replied, "His name is Haiyun.
Yun-lun was greatly astonished and said, "Mount Wutai is the dwelling place of Mañjuśrī.
The bhikṣu Haiyun is none other than the third spiritual friend encountered by Sudhana in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Why did you..."
"To abandon this Sage—after thousands and tens of thousands of kalpas, there is no way to encounter him even once. How grievous a mistake! Only then did Jie realize the truth of his origins.
He lamented that he could not shatter his own body and bones, yet in his foolish devotion, he still hoped to behold him again.
Consequently, he took leave of his family and returned to his former tracks, racing day and night until he reached his old place; however, he saw nothing at all. (From *Hongzan*, Fascicle 7.)

Haeshin requested to hear the account of Seol Eunggwang. He was a native of Silla. According to the *Liang Gongzhi Tu* (The Diagram of Tribute States under the Liang Dynasty), what was called Sulu during the Wei period was called Silla during the Song;

it was originally a state of the Dongyi (Eastern Barbarians) known as Jinkhan. Eunggwang came from a distinguished family lineage; he donned the monastic robes in his youth, and his insight and capacity were vast.

He was a man of transcendent caliber. Having been born and raised in a frontier region where the orthodox teaching had not yet spread, he arrived in the Wu and Kuaiji areas during the Renshou era of the Sui dynasty.

He encountered the Venerable Zhi when the latter was expounding the sublime scriptures. Guo devoted himself to him morning and evening, and within a few years, he suddenly attained great enlightenment.
Zhi then commissioned him to lecture on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; among the talented and brilliant disciples, there were none who did not submit in awe.

Later, while he was further cultivating the "Sublime Contemplation" (*miao guan*) at the separate cloister of Tiantai, he suddenly saw several people who said, "The Heavenly Emperor invites you to lecture.
Guo Guang silently consented; thereupon, his breath suddenly ceased. After ten days had passed, his complexion remained as usual, and he returned to his original consciousness.
Once his spiritual capacity and practice were perfected, he was about to return to his native country and boarded a large ship together with several dozen others.

Upon reaching the middle of the sea, the ship suddenly stopped moving. A man was seen riding a horse across the waves, coming to the bow of the ship and saying, "The Sea God invites the Master to visit his palace for a time to preach the Dharma.
Daoguang said, "This humble monk has vowed that this body shall always benefit sentient beings.

As for the ship and my fellow travelers, I do not yet know what will become of them. The man replied, "All people shall go along with you; do not worry about the ship. Thereupon, he raised [the vessel].
He descended with the multitude and walked several paces; he saw only a straight, level thoroughfare lined on both sides with fragrant flowers.

The Sea God, leading hundreds of thousands of attendants, welcomed him into his palace, where pearls and jade ornaments shone brilliantly, dazzling the eyes and mind. [The King] then preached the *Lotus Sūtra* once;
subsequently, vast treasures were bestowed upon him, and he was escorted back to his ship. The light reached his native land, and he propagated this scripture there ever after.

From his youth, he had recited and upheld [the scriptures] more than once a day; until the end of his life, this practice never faltered. When he reached nearly eighty years of age, he passed away at his residence.
After the cremation was completed, only his skull and tongue remained intact. Upon seeing and hearing this, the people of the entire country all marveled at such a rare occurrence.

Daokuang had two younger sisters who had long cherished pure faith. He took them in and provided for them with offerings. On several occasions he heard them reciting the *Lotus Sūtra* from memory, even from the "Chapter on the Stupa" to the "Chapter on the Encouragement of Devotion.
When his sisters encountered characters they did not recognize, they would ask him about them, and he would always explain them to them. (Recorded in the third fascicle of the *Hongzan fahua zhuan*).
A pigeon was reborn as a human being.
There was an old monk whose name has been lost, who resided at Shibi Temple in Bingzhou; he made the practice of meditative contemplation his vocation.

Toward the end of the Zhenguan era, two young pigeons appeared upon a beam of his chamber. The master would regularly feed them with leftover food. Although they gradually grew larger, [the account continues].
Their wings were not yet formed, yet they both attempted to fly; they fell together to the ground and died. The monk then collected their remains and buried them.
Ten days later, he dreamed at night that two small children told him: "We previously committed offenses and consequently received the bodies of pigeons.
Recently, we heard you reciting the Lotus Sūtra and have thus been able to receive human bodies. We are now [at a place] more than ten li from the side of the temple."
A certain man was conceived as a male child in the household of so-and-so in such-and-such a village; he was due to be born after ten months.
The monk went to visit him according to the appointed time and saw that a woman in this family had given birth to twin boys.

He attended their *pūrṇamāsa* (first-month) feast and called out to the two children, "Pigeon! Both responded, "Yes. After one of them had responded, it was not until more than a year later that they began to speak. [From] *Hongming ji*.
Eulogy IX: Shi Huiguo, who was liberated from the retribution of being a ghost in a latrine.
He was a native of Yuzhou. From his youth, he made his livelihood through ascetic practices. At the beginning of the Song dynasty, he traveled to the capital and arrived at Wa... [text fragment ends]
Guanshi used to recite the Lotus Sūtra at the temple. Once, he saw a ghost before the latrine who paid him homage and said, "In the past, I served as the *karmadāna* for the community of monks.
Because my conduct was slightly improper, I fell into this realm of ghosts who eat excrement. Your Eminence’s virtue and practice are lofty and brilliant, and your mind is set upon compassion;
I pray that you will assist me with a means to deliver me from here. He further said, "In the past, there was a man with money..."

Three thousand [coins] were buried beneath the roots of a persimmon tree. [Faguang] vowed to take them for the sake of merit. Guo immediately informed the assembly to dig them up; they indeed obtained three thousand.

He used them to produce a copy of the *Lotus Sūtra* and to convene a Dharma assembly. Later, he dreamed that this ghost said, "I have already attained rebirth, which is far superior to my former state.
Guo passed away in the sixth year of the Dashi era of the Song dynasty at the age of seventy-six.
Section Six: Extensive Praise. Section Eight:
The Chapter on Peaceful Conduct. The Dragons and Devas Request the Lecture;
Ghosts and Tigers Revere His Virtue; Immortals and Cranes Arrive in Grace; and the Wild Cock Transforms its Rebirth.
The water in his flask filled itself, a rare fragrance wafted everywhere, and light radiated from the script of the sutra; furthermore, the venom of a *visha* snake proved ineffective.

Long and heavenly beings requested him to expound the profound teachings. He was a native of Xiongchuan in the Eastern Sea (Korea). Crossing the vast ocean, he sought the methods of Chan in the Middle Kingdom. Upon hearing of Mount Heng...
Master Tanshi propagated both samādhi and prajñā and was also proficient in the Vinaya. With single-minded resolve, he traveled directly to Mount Nanyue.

There, [Huisi] contemplated his spiritual capacity and bestowed upon him the "Four Practices of Peaceful Bliss" from the Lotus Sūtra. His brilliance and benefit were like a divine awl; there was nothing solid that it could not penetrate.
He received [the teachings] and put them into practice, constantly cultivating diligence. Before long, he realized the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.
Sengyin said to him, "What you have realized is true and not false. You should return to your native land, employ skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), and propagate my teaching.
Guang bowed in prostration and took his leave. He then stayed in Jiangnan, boarded a ship, and reached the great ocean. There, he happened to see multicolored clouds and elegant music.

As he descended from the heights and arrived, a voice in the air said: "The Heavenly Emperor summons the Chan Master Xuanguang of海东 (Haidong) to the Dragon Palace to expound the Dharma-gate of Direct Realization.
Xuanguang folded his hands and declined, yet he saw only a youth in green robes leading the way as they entered the palace city.
It was unlike any human government office; the arrangement of its ceremonial guards consisted entirely of scaled creatures and spirits.

Once the Master had ascended the precious hall and subsequently climbed the high dais, he conversed as if in response to questions for seven days. When the proceedings were concluded, the Dragon King personally escorted him in farewell.
As Guāng boarded his boat again, the sailors remarked that it had been no more than half a day since they set sail upon the vast ocean. Guāng then arrived at his destination.
When the Elder Xiongchuan Wengshan tied his thatched hut and planted his monk’s staff there, those of like mind followed him, and thus a Buddhist monastery was established.
Among the twenty-eight worthies listed in the Ancestral Hall of Nanyue, Guang was one of them. This is recorded in the *Chuxian Yinglu*.
Guīhǔ Qīnfēng Shì Hóngmíng was a native of Shānyīn, Huìjī. He entered the monastic order at a young age and resided at Yúnmén Monastery in Shānyīn.

He recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and applied himself with diligence to ritual prostrations and repentance, never ceasing throughout the six periods of the day. Every morning, the water in his pitcher would fill itself; it was said that these were divine youths.
The Master considered him to be a servant. Once, while Ming was practicing *zazen* at Yunmen Temple, a tiger entered the main hall and crouched beneath his bed.
