At the age of twenty, he left the household life;
he immediately began reciting the Lotus Sūtra and attained ordination within several months. He chose to reside at Mount Zhongnan. His hair grew back immediately after being cut three times.
He vowed to recite [the scripture] one thousand times. He frequently experienced the miraculous occurrence of Guizi appearing in secret to protect him. Furthermore, he encountered deep snow;
having only about one *dou* of flour, he consumed it over more than twenty days without exhausting it.

Thereupon, he moved with his friend Lixin and a lay devotee to Hanshan, where they all built thatched huts and continued their former practice. Suddenly, a snake appeared, one hundred feet long and marked with five-colored patterns.
A snake, over ten feet tall, came directly to the hermitage, lowering its body and bowing its head to listen. At first, Daozhao was struck with alarm and trembling; he did not dare to look at it.
He gave rise to a heart of great compassion and made profound vows, joining his palms and shedding tears as he chanted the entire scripture aloud.
The snake withdrew after a short while. From then on, it came frequently and without ceasing. Although Daozhao knew well that it posed no harm, he loathed its stench.

[The monk] smelled [the creature] and, fearing its form, ordered the lay devotee (upāsaka) to drive it away. He then bound its neck with a rope, led it into a deep thicket, and tied it to a large tree.
That night, Daoxin and the lay devotee both dreamed of a woman who came forward weeping and covering her face, saying:
"I am a daughter of the mountain deity of this mountain. By nature, I delight in hearing the Dharma; yet because of my foul form, I have repeatedly intruded upon the Dharma."
"The assembly has now been driven away and bound; having taken leave of their teacher, they have gone far away and will no longer hear the recitation of the Mahāyāna.
This is what I regret. Zhào and the others were each startled awake and immediately questioned one another. Since their dreams were identical, they feared that [the monk] had died.

They at once took torches and went to look; indeed, such was the case. The layman called out in weeping and threw himself to the ground, confessing his sincerity and apologizing as he approached the corpse.
Together they recited the sutras. Furthermore, wishing to provide a vegetarian feast for a thousand monks, he obtained several silver ingots by the side of his hermitage;

descending the mountain to prepare the banquet, the provisions were exactly sufficient. Once, while traveling to a certain village, he was invited to stay and receive offerings by a poor woman named Liu.
The monk Śāṇakavāsin felt compassion for her and stayed. During those seven days, she exhausted all that she possessed. When Śāṇakavāsin wished to depart, the laywoman entreated him to remain.
Having no further goods, she cut off her hair to purchase food for the meal offering. After another seven days had passed, Śāṇakavāsin again wished to leave.
The poor woman wept bitterly and earnestly requested him to stay, so he remained once more. The woman used the proceeds from the sale of her hair for this purpose.
It was already gone. He remained in grief and resentment throughout the night, not knowing its whereabouts. Suddenly, he rubbed his head with his hand and felt that his hair had grown back as before.
Surprised and leaping for joy, he immediately cut it again. After another seven days, it grew long once more as it had been. This happened three times in total.
Zhao tried to detain him for a long time, but [Dao]zhi held his robes and bowl and resolutely refused to stay.

The woman then prostrated herself and spoke at length, saying, "The Master has his own provisions. When Zhao and the others heard this, they were choked with emotion and unable to speak; they lamented their own humble bodies in the face of such profound kindness.
In the Yongchun era, Zhao suddenly passed away without illness at Ganquan Temple. The fourfold assembly gathered wood and cremated him.

Only the tongue was not so; it remained red and raw as it had been before. The abbot of Qingxi Temple, Jieyin, and others, whose conduct was somewhat worldly and who did not believe such a thing could exist, then joined with five hundred monastics and laypeople from the entire temple, bringing several wagons of firewood and charcoal.
They burned it ten more times, yet its form and color remained unchanged. Only then did they all repent and submit.
His tongue was placed in an incense casket and circulated for offerings. (From *Hongzan*, fascicle 8.)
Section Ten: Chapter on Never-Disparaging; Chapter on the Tathāgata’s Supernatural Powers; Chapter on the Entrustment.
Mushrooms sprout beside the tomb, lotuses emerge from the tongue-root, and śarīra relics flow forth as golden script, their radiance illuminating the jeweled stupa.
The lay devotee Wei Zhonggui, a native of Linqiong, was by nature filial and fraternal. During the Wude era, his father fell ill. The water in his pitcher remained warm in winter and cold in summer;

celestial soldiers filled the earth and the sky; and *zhī* fungi grew beside his grave. (Note: The term "lay devotee" translates *qingxinshi*, referring to a Buddhist lay follower who maintains pure faith.)
Zhonggui was diligent in his filial care. Upon the death of his father, he sent away his wife and concubines and lived in a thatched hut to the left of the grave.
He was particularly devoted to Buddhism and recited the *Lotus Sūtra*. By day he carried earth to build the mound, and by night he recited the sūtra, persevering with tireless diligence.
Fierce beasts often came to the front of his hut at night; they crouched there listening to the sutras for a long time before departing.

Zhonggui maintained a state of right mindfulness and said, "I do not wish for fierce beasts to press upon me. The beasts then rose and left. The following morning, he saw seventy-three stalks of *zhicao* (fungus/herb) growing around the tomb;
those in front of the grave were arranged in orderly rows as if planted by humans, all with vermilion stems.
A purple canopy appeared; the diameter of the canopy was five inches, and its luster was extraordinary. The neighbors reported this to the prefecture and county authorities.
At that time, Zheng Junchang was serving as the Regional Inspector (Cishi) and Xue Yu was serving as the Adjutant (Biejia). Together they went to the site of the tomb to sigh in admiration.

They gathered *zhicao* fungi and submitted a memorial to the throne requesting that the family’s gate be honored. Their final whereabouts were unknown. [This account is] from the eighth fascicle of the *Hongzan*.
Lianchu Shigeng, whose secular surname was Yang, resided at Changle Temple in Yangzhou. He was diligent in his observance of the precepts and recited the Lotus Sūtra.
Toward the end of the Daye era of the Sui dynasty, Yuwen Huaji committed a rebellion in Yangzhou and murdered Emperor Yang within the palace.
At that time, the empire was in chaos and the common people suffered from famine; a single *dou* of rice cost ten thousand coins.

Zhìyè was then staying in a separate courtyard, dwelling in a small hut where he recited [the scriptures] incessantly. He subsequently starved to death inside his room, and no one took him to be buried.
Consequently, the hut collapsed, and his remains remained beneath it. Following the pacification at the beginning of the Yínníng era, his...
Suddenly, a single lotus stalk sprang up from the ground, its radiance and color extraordinary. Monastics and laypeople alike were struck with wonder and sighed in amazement, none knowing the cause.
At that time, an elder monk of the temple spoke, saying: "In this place, there will once have been a monk who specialized in reciting the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Since those were times of war and chaos, he passed away here and was left unburied; his remains must surely be here. This is certainly that monk."
This was his spiritual power. Thereupon, they sought out and excavated the roots of the flowers. The blue lotus had grown from beneath the tongue within the skull;

the tongue was as if still alive, completely unrotted and undecayed. The monastic community then took the tongue and the flower up to the hall, where they struck the bell to assemble the multitude for the recitation of the *Lotus Sūtra*.
As the scripture was being chanted, the tongue continued to vibrate. Those among both the clergy and the laity who heard this and witnessed it were moved.
The crowd stood as if in a wall; there was none who did not sigh in admiration, and all gave rise to the supreme resolve (*anuttara-saṃbodhi-citta*).
This concludes the seventh section on "Extensive Praise. Regarding Śarīra:

its manifestation in golden script was explained by Zhìyǎn. He was a native of the same prefecture. At the age of thirteen, he suddenly encountered a Brahman monk and entered the monastic life, abiding in the precepts and his religious duties.
At the temple, he studied the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Vimalakīrti*, the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and other sūtras extensively, thoroughly mastering their definitive meanings (*nītārtha*).
He subsequently became a master of the Dharma, truly a "Dharma Master of Noble Purity" whose conduct and speech were both perfected.

In the third year of the Xianqing era, the monastics and laypeople of Daozhu County in Taizhou invited Huian to lecture on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* at Lingshan Temple. As Huian was returning to his incense chamber from the temple monks...
While staying in his residence, during the first watch of the night, he took the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and spread it out upon his desk, intending to read it.

At that time, the incense burner and his three attendants were all present there. Before he had even finished solemnly burning the incense, he suddenly saw three śarīra relics emerge from the character for "Buddha" (*buddha*) on the sūtra.
Five-colored light radiated and filled the entire sūtra, circulating without ceasing, and then returned [to their source].
The monks were summoned by the incense and all came together to pay their respects, wishing to collect the śarīra.
The śarīra flowed back into the Buddha-character. The monks prostrated themselves and wept with grief, burning incense and making vows to behold the true countenance once more.
The śarīra emerged again from within the Buddha-character, circulating without ceasing; in a brief moment, it appeared within another Buddha-character.

He subsequently withdrew into seclusion. He solemnly lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra* some dozens of times. The spiritual responses and auspicious omens he experienced are difficult to describe in detail.
For several days prior to his passing, he traveled from place to place, bidding farewell to each of his Dharma friends and old acquaintances.
Suddenly, one day, after sweeping the courtyard, he sat upright in meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and passed away. Immediately, a wondrous fragrance filled the entire courtyard.
After seven more days had passed, several years following his death, his tongue remained undecayed; his hair and beard had grown two inches longer, and his complexion was as it had been before.
Those who recognized him considered him to be one of those who had attained the Way. (From *Hongzan*, fascicle 3.)
The Radiant Illumination Shines Upon the Treasure Stupa:

Xiao Yu, Duke of Song and Vice President of the Left. His courtesy name was Shimu. His great-grandfather was Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty; his father was Emperor Ming. The Duke had deep faith in the Buddhist scriptures.

Whenever he attended banquets or assemblies, the Emperor would invariably issue an imperial decree for him to be separately granted vegetarian fare. Although the Duke participated in state affairs, [he remained steadfast in his devotion].

He recited and chanted without fail. He produced the *Fahua yiji* (Record of the Meaning of the Lotus Sutra) in ten fascicles. At that time, he lectured upon the fourth [fascicle] for his sons and nephews.
On the day the commentary was completed, he dreamed that the Stūpa of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna shone brilliantly in the sky.
Consequently, he summoned skilled artisans to construct this wondrous stūpa. (From *Hongzan*, Fascicle 3).
The ācārya of Changgan Temple to the east [maintained] a water jar that was warm in winter and cold in summer. He recited the Lotus Sūtra and possessed great integrity and conduct;
whenever he recited it, the water in his jar would become warm in winter and cold in summer as a regular sign. (Cited from *Hongzan* 7.)

Shi Xuanshou, whose name was Tianbing Zadi Yingkong, entered the monastic life as a youth and resided at Suihua Temple in Huangzhou. He constantly recited the Lotus Sūtra and frequently experienced miraculous manifestations.
It was the height of the summer heat. His companions, seeking coolness, sent for Sengxiu, wishing to engage him in conversation.

When he arrived before the chamber, he saw only a solemn and imposing array of attendants and a grand retinue of men and horses; terrified, he returned and reported this. His companions went together to observe, and it was exactly as before, no different.
As they moved toward the rear gate, his followers became even more numerous. Looking up into the air, it was filled to the horizon with those riding upon—

Elephants and horses appeared, mingled with various ghosts and spirits; only then did he realize their spiritual resonance and communication. He set them aside and subsequently withdrew from the world. At dawn the next morning, he felt ashamed and apologized [to his teacher], whereupon his circle of disciples was severed.

Daoshou devoted himself exclusively to this practice and lived until the end of the Sui dynasty at the temple. This concludes the seventh fascicle of the *Chū Hongzan* (Excerpts from the Propagation and Praise).
Section Twelve: The Chapter on the Past Deeds of Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva.
He himself recognized his former life; the two characters "difficult" and "penetration" [were inscribed]. Sandalwood fragrance reached him from afar, and the Buddha’s hand personally touched him.
The essence of the medicine entered his womb; he was healed by the water of the pond. His leprosy sores were immediately cured, and his vital strength increased and flourished.
Acute illnesses were thereby cured, and severe wind-ailments were likewise benefited.

He himself recognized his previous life as Cui Yanwu, the Prefect of Wei Prefecture during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty. While traveling through the commandery on official business, he arrived at a certain district and suddenly said:
The attendant said, "In the past, I was a woman living in this town; now I know my former dwelling place.

Thereupon, she mounted her horse and followed the winding alleys until she reached a house, where she ordered the gate to be knocked. An elderly man, the master of the house, opened the door and invited her inside.
She ascended the hall and sat down. The old man asked, "For what purpose has the official come here? Wu immediately replied, "In my previous life, I was you."

The old man asked, "By what means may this be verified? Wu replied, "In the past, while I was reciting the Lotus Sūtra, I hid five gold hairpins inside the eastern wall at a height of six or seven feet from the ground; that is where they are located.
Furthermore, there is one page missing from the end of the seventh fascicle of that sūtra due to fire damage, and as I recite it now, I constantly forget that passage."

"It was lost," [he said]. He had people bore a hole high up through the wall, and indeed they found the scripture; although the paper had been damaged by fire, they also recovered a gold hairpin, exactly as he had said.
The host wept and said, "While my deceased wife was alive, she constantly recited this scripture, and the gold hairpin was also hers.
Yenwu spoke again, saying, "The locust tree in front of the courtyard—the place where I placed my loosened hair when I was born in the past—"
He sent someone to search for it, and indeed found the hair. Upon seeing this, the host was filled with a mixture of grief and joy.
Wu then left his clothing and belongings as a gift and departed. (From the *Lingshui ji*, *Hongzan zhuan*, and *Xianying lu*).
He could not master two characters in a certain passage and lost their names. He resided at Dongsi Temple in Qin Commandery.

There was a śrāmaṇera who recited the Lotus Sūtra with great fluency, yet whenever he reached the two characters "Āi-dài" (靉靆) in the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter, he would forget them as soon as they were taught. This happened up to a thousand times; the Master grew weary of it.
He scolded him, saying, "Since you have mastered this entire *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* so thoroughly, how could you not be able to focus your mind on remembering these two characters?
That night, the Master dreamed of a monk who said to him, "You should not scold him.

This śrāmaṇera was in his previous life a laywoman (*upāsikā*) in the eastern village by the temple; he originally recited the entire *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, but because of his family's customs..."
In the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter of the *Huā* (Flower) version of the sutra, the two characters "Āi-dài" (靉靆) were omitted where they appear in the "White Fish" (白魚) version.

At that time, these two characters were not present in the sutra text; this was merely because [the former] had recently received it in this life and his practice was not yet perfected. His name was so-and-so, and the sutra is still extant today.
If anyone does not believe this, they may go and verify it for themselves. The Master went to that village the following morning to inquire about this household, saying:
Bi asked the host what scriptures he possessed. The host replied that he had one copy of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Bi requested it to examine it;

he found that two characters were missing from the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter. Upon inquiry, he learned that they were characters his deceased daughter’s wife had been reciting and upholding during her lifetime.
It has been calculated that he passed away seventeen years ago; indeed, this corresponds exactly to the year, month, and lunar day of this śrāmaṇera’s birth.
Nothing further is known of the śrāmaṇera’s final end. Excerpted from the sixth fascicle of the *Hongzan*.
The Master of Sandalwood Fragrance Who Reached Afar was named Guanding. The King of Wuyue posthumously conferred upon him the title Zongchi. He was born into the Wu clan of Zhang’an;

at the age of three, he was already able to recite the names of the Triple Gem alongside his mother. He received the teachings of meditative concentration and wisdom from Tiantai, and later arrived at Chengxin.
At the vihāra, he lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra* for a long time, and his transformative influence spread among the worldly laity.

At that time, there was a villager from Falong Village, thirty *li* away from the mountain, who fell ill and was near death. His son rushed there to seek salvation; the Master recited the *Lotus Sūtra* for him and burned sandalwood incense.
The patient smelled the fragrance from afar and was immediately healed. (Recorded in the *Hongzan* [Biographies of Eminent Monks], fascicle 3, and the *Xianyingshuo lu*).

The Buddha’s hand personally stroked the head of Luo Yu of the Song dynasty and his wife, Lady Fei, who was from Ningzhou. Lady Fei had deep faith and reverence for the Triple Gem and recited the Lotus Sūtra;
for several years she practiced with diligence and without slackening. Suddenly, she fell ill with a heartache that gradually turned into a high fever. Her entire family...
Terrified and anxious, he muttered to himself: "I have recited the sutras with diligent toil; surely there must be some virtuous protection. I shall certainly not meet my death because of this.
Soon after, as he lay down to sleep, that very night the Buddha extended his hand through the window and rubbed his heart.
Both inside and out, the entire room was filled with golden light, and a wondrous fragrance wafted in. From then on, his illness was cured. Those who saw it could not [fail to marvel].
He did not produce faith. This appears in the *Hongzan* (Volume 6) and the *Xianyingshu*.
Yijingruohuai, whose secular name was Jingjian, is unknown as to where he was from. He entered the monastic order in his childhood and resided frequently at Chonggao and Longmen.
Shan recited the Lotus Sūtra thirteen thousand times. As he had been reciting and upholding it for a long time, his physical strength became exhausted.
More than twenty years later, he suddenly heard the clamorous chatter of several children to the north of his dwelling.
He felt increasingly distressed and could not discern where the children were coming from. There was an old man with white hair wearing white...
Wearing a training skirt and tunic, he would inquire at every visit, "How are the four elements of the Chan Master? The Master replied, "I am gradually feeling more emaciated and exhausted.
He added, "I do not know where so many small children have come from; they trouble me day after day until it can no longer be endured. The old man said:

The Master went to the place where they were playing and sat down, waiting for them to take off their clothes and enter the water to bathe. As they did so, the Master followed and took back the clothes of one small boy.
If anyone came to retrieve them, he was cautioned not to give them back. If the boy should scold the Master, he was cautioned not to respond; instead, the disciple should go and speak to him himself.
Seeing that he followed the old man, the boy spoke and went to wait for him. The other boys indeed took off their clothes and entered the water.
After bathing in the pond, he took the young child’s clothes back to his room. The child soon followed him, searching for his garments.

Seeing this, he recalled the old man’s words of instruction that they were never to be returned. The child immediately began to speak with foul language, slandering the Zen Master and his ancestral lineage.
The Master did not respond. The white-haired old man soon arrived and said to the child, "Enter into the Master’s embrace. At first, the child...
He was unwilling to comply. After the old man had urged and pressed him several times, he finally entered and saw Huai, who was submerged within his belly.
The old man asked the Master, "How are your four elements? Huai replied, "My strength is superior to what it has been before. The old man departed shortly thereafter;

from that time on, his physical strength became robust and he recited [the scriptures] many times over. Those who recognized him said, "This must have been the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra causing the mountain..."
A deity drove forth the essence of various medicinal herbs and transformed them into small children, causing him to consume them so as to eliminate his illnesses.
After this was seen, nothing further is known of his end. This is recorded in the sixth fascicle of the *Hongzan*.

Shi Sengming, who used the water of a pond to treat illnesses, resided at Shimen Mountain in Haozhou. At the summit of the mountain, he constructed a Maitreya Heavenly Palace out of piled bricks and a statue of Maitreya.
He constantly recited the Lotus Sūtra, and frequently heard the sound of fingers snapping and voices calling out from the air.
"Excellent! she cried. During the Tianjian era, she repeatedly submitted petitions to Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty requesting permission to immolate herself by fire.
Only after her pleas had been made three times did she finally receive his consent. She then fulfilled her long-held vow upon a stone slab in front of the Maitreya Hall;

her body was completely reduced to ashes, leaving behind only a single fingernail. Once the cremation was finished, the ground where she lay, measuring four or five feet, suddenly sank to form a pond. After two nights, flowers bloomed there.
Its fresh growth flourishes beyond compare. Those who drink from its pools are all cured of their illnesses. Later generations fashioned a small image and re-fired these shells;
they used the ashes to smear it. Whenever anyone defiled the image, it would immediately move away.
Along the paths where people practiced the Way, flowers grew everywhere, as large as pears or jujubes, numbering over a thousand. A stupa currently stands there, fully commemorating these events.
Fifth, Record of Propagation and Praise:
The Healing of Leprosy.
At Qianquan Temple on Mount Gu in Jiangzhou during the Tang dynasty, there was Chan Master Fache. While walking in the mountains, he encountered a man suffering from leprosy.
While living in an earthen cave, he begged for food from his teacher. The teacher took pity on him, led him back to the monastery, and further dug an earthen cell for him to dwell in.

He provided him with clothing and food and taught him to recite the *Lotus Sūtra*. Although the man was originally illiterate and moreover vulgar, the teacher instructed him word by word without ever growing weary.
When he had recited about half of it, he suddenly dreamed of a monk who gave him instruction; from that time on...

Gradually his intelligence and wisdom awakened. By the time he reached the fifth or sixth fascicle, the sores on his body gradually subsided; he mastered the entire scripture, and his four elements were restored to health.
Thus, the Buddha’s words regarding the excellent medicine for illness were proven true. (From the *Lingrui ji*, Hongzan, section 8, and the *Xianying lu*).

His physical strength increased significantly, bringing joy to the monastic community. He left the household life and resided at Zhicheng Temple in Jinling. Originally suffering from chronic weakness and lacking physical vigor, he resolved his heart upon the temple pagoda to perform repentance.
With earnest and sincere prayers, he recited the *Lotus Sūtra* without ceasing for a short period of time.
His strength surged with vigor. Before the temple pagoda stood two stone lions, both of immense size and weight.
Senghuang suddenly thrust both arms under the bellies of the lions and lifted them up, running off. He traveled for about ten *li* without feeling the slightest fatigue.
Sixth, the account of Zhao Chen, who was cured of a sudden and severe illness through the propagation of [the Dharma].
Zhao Chen was by nature upright and steadfast, yet he unfortunately suffered from a sudden, acute ailment. Although he underwent various treatments, not a single one proved effective.
It was effective. He then resolved his will to recite the Lotus Sūtra, and his illness was suddenly cured. From that time on, he constantly recited it without slackening.

He subsequently joined with the monks Yin-yang and Ri-zi, as well as Yan-yuan and several others, both monastics and laypeople, to form a fellowship of the Lotus Sūtra, collectively cultivating the Buddha-wisdom.
Dafeng Yili, whose original name has been lost, was a man of unknown origin. Unluckily, he contracted black leprosy, for which no remedy could be found despite every effort.

Suddenly, he heard that the *Lotus Sūtra* is the excellent medicine for the ailments of those in Jambudvīpa. He vowed to recite it in its entirety, and his illness was subsequently cured. Furthermore—
There was a Mr. Liu, the Recorder of Nantai, who also contracted this illness. Although he treated it in various ways, there was no efficacy.
One day, while on an unnamed road, he encountered [the deity] and [the deity] said: "I too once suffered from this disease; by relying on the recitation of the Lotus Sutra, I was immediately cured."
Thereupon, Lady Liu gave rise to resolute faith. She immediately sought out the Lotus Sutra and held the scroll in her hands without releasing it until she had completed the entire work.
Suddenly, she dreamed that a strange monk rubbed her body with his hand; she then applied moxibustion all over her body using mugwort cones.

Startled, she woke up immediately, with perspiration flowing like a stream. Her body and mind became suddenly clear and expansive, as if parting through clouds and mist; she was restored to her former state.
Section Thirteen: The Chapter on Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara;
the deceased mother is liberated from suffering; divine beings dwell in the air; water cannot float the corpse; no stench arises;
the tiger’s roar repels the bandits; the characters transform into gold.
My late mother was liberated from suffering.
In Chang’an, there was Liu Gongxin of Tongzhuang; his wife, née Chen, had previously died of illness.
Later, Chen suddenly passed away and saw a man lead her into hell, where she witnessed all manner of scenes of retribution for sins. Afterwards, she saw a prison with a stone gate.

Suddenly, it opened. Inside, her mother was undergoing extreme suffering. Seeing her daughter, the mother said, "You should copy one volume of the Lotus Sūtra for me so that I may be delivered from this.
Having spoken, the door closed. Lady Chen revived once more and recounted this; Xu Gong believed her.
She immediately relied upon her brother-in-law, Zhao Shizi, to transcribe this scripture. Suddenly, a professional scribe arrived carrying a newly transcribed copy of the *Lotus Sūtra* for sale.
Zhao said, "Fortunately, we have this very scripture; you may redeem it instead. There is no need to transcribe another. Liu followed his advice and gave the new copy to Lady Chen.
One day, while Lady Chen was preparing food for her mother, she dreamed that her mother said to her, "I previously instructed you to transcribe [the scripture]."
"There is a scripture in one fascicle; why do you not obtain it for me? The daughter replied, "I have already finished redeeming one fascicle.

The mother said, "Because of this scripture, I shall incur even heavier retribution. The jailer beat my back until it was broken because I did not agree to take the scripture from the Fan family as my own property.

Upon waking from her dream, the daughter hurriedly requested someone to transcribe it. When the scripture was completed, she dreamed again that her mother informed her: "I have received the scripture."

[He] has already been liberated from the Office of Darkness and is dwelling in peace in a good realm. He has now come to inform you; you should believe this with a sincere heart and dwell well in the world.
Furthermore, upon inquiring about the aforementioned scripture, it was indeed written by a person surnamed Fan during the Longshuo era of the Tang dynasty.
This is extracted from the *Fayuan zhulin* (Forest of Gems in the Garden of the Dharma), compiled by Shi Daoshi, which consists of one hundred fascicles and is included in the canon.
Shenren Zhukong (釋玄真) was a native of Shouchun. He resided at Yongfu Temple and recited the *Lotus Sūtra* without ceasing at any time.
Once, during an autumn night under the moon, as he was reciting this sūtra, he reached the middle of the seventh fascicle when a novice from a neighboring room appeared.
As he was about to rise from his seat to go to the toilet, he saw the shadow of a giant figure in the courtyard.
He raised his head and looked around, and immediately beheld a divine being standing majestically in the air. This śramaṇa stood still in his place and gazed up at him, not taking another step.
After a long while, when the scripture had been finished, the spirit suddenly vanished. From that time on, the monk began to learn how to recite it.
He maintained this throughout his life without slackening. (From *Hongzan*, fascicle 8).
During the Wude era of the Tang dynasty, Su Chang was appointed as the Prefect of Bazhou. Accompanied by his family, he traveled to take up his post; while crossing the Jialing River...
In the middle of the Yangtze River, a wind arose and the ship’s sails were overturned and submerged. More than sixty men and women perished all at once.
There was only one female servant who constantly recited the *Lotus Sūtra*. As the waves surged into the boat, the woman placed the scripture case upon her head and vowed to perish with it.
Immediately, she did not sink; she floated along with the waves and reached the shore in an instant. She then carried the case up onto the bank.

Upon opening and inspecting the scripture, it was found to be completely free of moisture. This woman later married a man from a certain place in Yangzhou; her devotion and her recitation of the scriptures became even more profound than they had been before.
This account appears in the *Fayuan zhulin* (Forest of Gems in the Garden of the Dharma), as well as in the ninth fascicle of the *Hongzan* and the *Xianying lu* (Record of Manifested Responses).

Shi Bushengxiu Daoshi, whose secular surname was Shi and his given name Chong, was a native of the southern suburbs of Chang’an. He had belonged to the Daoist order from a young age and early on joined the Yellow Turban rebels.

He resided at Xuandu Guan, where he later suddenly resolved to recite the *Lotus Sūtra*, doing so once every day. He also privately established an image of the Buddha and performed worship during the six periods of the day.
He performed rites and repentances, for which he was constantly envied by followers of other paths. Because of this, he returned to secular life and became even more diligent in his recitations.

Later, he suddenly fell ill and passed away during the height of summer; yet his body showed no signs of decay, and only a fragrant scent was perceived. His relatives held him in high esteem and carved a niche in the wall beside their residence to enshrine him.
From time to time, they would always smell a wondrous fragrance. After several years had passed, all his flesh and sinews had completely vanished, leaving only the shape of his tongue.
His complexion was no different from that of ordinary people. Some were filled with doubt and alarm, yet he remained unchanged when burned by fire and suffered no injury when struck with an axe.
Those who saw or heard of this from near and far came to believe him a hundredfold more than before. (From *Hongzan*, Fascicle 8.)
Huhou Tuize Shi Fa’ai was a native of Changsha. He recited the Lotus Sūtra and traveled to Jiaozhi on account of certain circumstances.
Encountering a rebellion by the people of Jiaozhi, Fa’ai hid himself in accordance with local custom. Suddenly, he was captured by five bandits and placed in one location; they said, "Wait for us."
After they had finished eating, they killed the practitioner. Huai then saw a spear by the wall; he took it up and went outside, running straight toward the north.
When the bandits finished eating and rose, they saw Huai from afar and rushed forward in pursuit. Upon reaching a thorn bush, Huai threw himself inside to hide.
There he encountered two tigers lying together in an embrace; when the tigers saw Huai approaching, they both raised their heads.
When Ai saw the tigers, she became terrified and said, "O two donors, I have been pursued by bandits and am fleeing in haste to seek refuge with you;
I pray that you will receive and protect me. The two tigers immediately went outside, lashing their tails and roaring fiercely, whereupon the bandits retreated and dispersed.
Ai fled further north, followed by the tigers. Upon reaching the bank of a river, she saw a man holding several pieces of food and drink, which he gave to her.
He ate it with relish; its flavor was most exquisite. He then crossed the water to an island, whereupon the tiger also left him and departed.

He remained overnight on the island. There he encountered two other men and stayed with them for the night as well. They prepared a great variety of rare delicacies, and only at dawn did they part ways.
He further instructed them, saying, "Simply travel toward the north, and you shall surely escape. Thereupon, having traveled over thirty li to the north, he encountered—
An old acquaintance saw him and rejoiced; only then was he able to escape. Later, Ai recounted this to both monastics and laypeople, but it is unknown where he ended up.
This is extracted from the seventh fascicle of the *Hongzan*.
Zi-hua was surnamed Jin Zhang Wanfu.
During the Zhenguan era, he served as the Prefect of Luozhou. By nature he was coarse and fierce, and he did not particularly respect or believe in the Dharma.
Upon first arriving at his post, he inquired of those around him which monks within his jurisdiction possessed virtuous conduct. His attendants replied:

Below Kuò there was a nun named Miaozhì who was extremely diligent. She had also produced a copy of the *Lotus Sūtra* (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*), which she upheld and made offerings to according to the Dharma.
Because of this, her reputation filled the local villages. Wàn Fú attempted to send an official to seek out the scripture and examine it.

When the nun heard that the Regional Inspector (*cìshǐ*) was seeking the scripture, she refused to give it up, saying, "The Magistrate does not maintain ritual purity, nor has he fasted or purified himself. Wàn...
Wanfu became greatly incensed. He sent another person to fetch it; the nun did not dare to detain him and immediately handed over the scripture for him to take.

Once Wanfu obtained the scripture, he failed to wash his hands before taking it up and opening the scroll. Inside, the paper was entirely yellow, and there was not a single character to be found. Wanfu was then filled with great rage.
He said, "This is a wicked old nun. How can she be tolerated? He immediately ordered his attendants to pursue and bring the nun before him. He sent a messenger to tell the nun:

"In the sutra you have recited, there is not a single word [of the original]. The Magistrate is greatly incensed and has ordered your pursuit. The nun was filled with great anxiety and fear, not knowing the cause;
her sweat flowed down her entire body as she followed the messenger to the gate of the Prefect’s office. She entered through the inner courtyard wall.
The nun saw two Vajrapāṇis holding vajras and clubs, appearing as if they were bestowing them upon her; her mind was thus set at ease.

She immediately entered into the presence of the Prefect, whereupon the text of the scripture transformed into golden letters suspended in mid-air. When the Prefect saw the nun arrive, [he beheld this marvel].

He also saw vajras and golden characters suspended in the void. Thereupon, struck with alarm and fear, he rose and fled from the hall, wailing and weeping bitterly as he offered apologies, performed repentance, and prostrated himself.

He immediately turned his mind toward faith, vowing to have one thousand copies of the Lotus Sūtra transcribed for universal offering throughout the ten directions, while he himself maintained the practice without daring to be indolent. This was from the Prefectural Governor.
After they had taken refuge [in the Dharma], everyone took the Lotus Sūtra as their primary practice. Wanfu then inquired about the process of producing the paper for the sūtras.
The nun replied: "When I wished to produce the sūtras, I first planted grain trees in the mountains and irrigated them with scented water to ensure their growth.
Once the trees were mature, I used scented water mixed with mud to construct a house of paper, and then I harvested the grain."
[They] hired craftsmen to manufacture paper according to the Dharma using fragrant water for purification. They sought out individuals capable of maintaining ritual purity to serve as scribes.
Later, a man from Jiangnan, approximately twenty-four or twenty-five years of age, responded to the call to write.
The scripture hall was likewise constructed with mud mixed with fragrant water to ensure purity. Before beginning the transcription, the scribe donned new, clean robes. Prior to writing the sutra...
For forty-nine days, maintain the pure fast (*śīla*). Only then begin the transcription. Each time a scroll is finished, change your clothes and bathe;
only after this is done may you return to the transcription. While transcribing, the nun shall hold an incense burner and kneel on her right knee before the scripture to make offerings to the scribe.
Do not let these rites be omitted. When the scripture is completed and its adornment is perfected, one then prepares the fourfold assembly of monks, nuns, men, and women.
Each person was provided with ten sets of robes. Whenever someone came to borrow scriptures, they were first instructed to observe ritual purity for seven days and were given new clothes to wear;
only then were the scriptures handed over. By treating them with such reverence, the tradition was never deficient or interrupted. (From *Hongzan*, Chapter 10.)
Section Fourteen: The Universal Gate Chapter.
The Dharma-wisdom of a śramaṇa cannot be burned by fire. When he was a layman, he was traveling alone through a vast marsh when fierce fires broke out simultaneously on all four sides.
Knowing he was certain to die, he pressed his face to the ground and invoked Avalokiteśvara with a sincere heart. To his amazement, the fire did not reach him.
When he raised his head to look, all the grass in the marsh, down to the finest fibers, was consumed by the flames; yet the spot of ground where he lay prostrate remained unburnt.

Through this experience, he attained spiritual awakening and renounced the secular life to become a monk. This account is taken from the "Biography of Xie Fu" in the Jin Dynasty, titled *The Biography of Avalokiteśvara*.
Cen Wénbèn, the Minister of the Central Secretariat, was a native of Jiangling. From his youth, he harbored upright faith and constantly recited the "Universal Gate" chapter of the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Once, while crossing the Wú Sōng River, a wind arose in midstream and both man and boat were submerged. Wénbèn floated upon the surface of the water and heard—
A human voice said, "If you merely recite the Buddha's name and chant the sutras, you will certainly not die. This was said three times.

From then on, he followed the waves until he reached the shore. Later, when a vegetarian feast was held in Jiangling, the assembly of monks gathered together; there was one monk who arrived alone and late.
The *Wenben* said: "The world is currently in turmoil; may you, sir, fortunately avoid harm and encounter a great era of peace, thereby attaining wealth and honor.
Having spoken these words, he departed. Suddenly, at one time, Wenben found a grain of *śarīra* soil within his food bowl.
That he attained a great era of peace and wealth and honor was exactly as the monk had said. This is recorded in the *Lingshui ji* and the *Xianying lu*.
Furthermore, in Hai Lan County, there was a man who fell into the water. His companions all drowned, but this man called upon Avalokiteśvara and happened upon a stone.
Exhausted, he drifted as if asleep; then he saw two people on a boat calling for him to come aboard. When he opened his eyes, he indeed saw the men and the boat, which carried him away.
Having reached the shore, they were no longer seen. This is excerpted from the biography of Xie Fu.

More than a hundred foreigners, having escaped the peril of rākṣasas, were traveling from Siṃhala toward Funan when they were suddenly struck by a violent wind and fell into the land of ghosts. The ghosts...
He was about to eat [the man]. The crowd on the boat, struck with fear, invoked the name of Guanyin. Among them was a śramaṇa of the Hīnayāna who, lacking faith, did not invoke it.
The ghost then seized him; he was terrified and called out the name, and was likewise saved. This is excerpted from Shi Fu’s *Biographies of Guanyin*.
A black wind blew their ship.
At that time in Silla, there was a woman named P’ohe who resided in the Golden Ward (Kumgang-bang) of the royal capital. She had a son named Changchun.
He set sail upon the sea with a merchant vessel, but when the appointed time had passed, his whereabouts remained unknown. He brooded over him morning and night until he grew emaciated.
Fortunately, he heard of the power of the Universal Gate to manifest supernatural transformations:

"Even if a black wind should blow their ship and cast them adrift into the land of the rākṣasa demons, by invoking His name, they shall immediately attain liberation. Thereupon, he conceived deep faith and went to the Minzang Temple.
Before the statue of Avalokiteśvara at the temple, she prayed with diligent devotion for approximately seven days. On the seventh day, she suddenly felt Changchun take her mother’s hand;

she was both startled and joyful, weeping as she did so. The temple monks questioned her in wonder about the cause of this. Changchun said, "When I left home to cross the sea, I suddenly encountered a violent storm.
All those on the same ship were buried in the bellies of fish, yet I alone, riding upon a single plank, reached Wu. Wu...
A man captured me as a slave and made me plow the wild fields. Suddenly, a strange monk came and said to me, "Do you remember your country?
I immediately knelt and replied, "I have an elderly mother there; my longing for her is boundless. The monk said, "If you wish to see your mother, follow me.
Having spoken, he walked eastward, and I followed him. There was a ditch, and the monk took my hand and leaped across it. It was dark.
I was as if in a dream. Suddenly, I heard my mother’s voice. Upon arriving before the image at Minjang Temple, although I recognized her clearly as my mother, I still suspected it was a dream.
Thus, on the eighth day of the fourth month in the year of Yiyou (the fourth year of the Tianbao era), I departed from Wu at the hour of Shen and arrived in this hall at the hour of Xu.
King Jeongde heard of this and held me in high esteem, bestowing generous gifts and provisions to ensure that offerings would be maintained forever.
On the eighth day of every month, he would visit the temple to pay homage and offer praise; this was established as a permanent practice.

Bao Kai made an agreement with Changchun to organize the laymen and laywomen of the neighborhood into a community of pure faith (*śraddhā-vat*), specifically commissioning one copy of the *Lotus Sūtra* written in golden characters.

Whenever the third month of spring arrived, they would establish a *dharmapūjā* site (*maṇḍala*) to proclaim the sublime principles and cultivate worship with diligence, looking upward to repay the profound grace [of the Buddhas]. (Recorded from the Xuzang jing)
The temple records, as well as the *Gujiji* (Ancient Records) of Goryeo, the *Lüezhuan* (Brief Biographies),
and the *Honglu* (Extensive Records),
further state that during the Taizhong era of the Jin dynasty, a man from Pengcheng was falsely accused of being a bandit. This man had previously made offerings to a golden image.

He wore it within his topknot. Later, when he was subjected to the law and stood beneath the blade, he heard a golden sound. Although the blade struck his neck three times, there was ultimately no injury.
Upon examining it, the image bore three marks. Because of this, he was spared from punishment. This is recorded in the *Shēfū Guānyīn Zhuàn* (Biography of Guānyīn by Xiè Fū).

There was also Gaojian. When he was about to be executed for violating the law, he single-mindedly took refuge in the Buddha. As the blade descended, it snapped; when they attempted to strangle him, his body broke into pieces.
He then sold his wife and children as well as himself to raise funds to erect a five-story stupa.
The shackles and chains fell away of their own accord.

During the Jin dynasty, there was Zhang Chang, who served as the Senior Counselor (Changshi) to Prince Xiao. When the Prince and Chang were imprisoned in the Court of Judicial Review (Tingwei) due to certain affairs, Chang had long possessed upright faith;
he immediately resolved his mind to recite the "Universal Gate" chapter of the *Lotus Sūtra* one thousand times in order to seek release. As he maintained this mindfulness...

Upon the completion of these words, the shackles and chains were instantly broken and destroyed, and both men were liberated. This is recorded in the *Biography of Xie Fu* (Shè Fū Guānyīn Zhuàn) and the *Record of Manifested Responses* (Xiàn Yìng Lù) from the Jin Dynasty. Furthermore...
Gaihu was a native of Shanyang. He was imprisoned and sentenced to death. For three days and three nights, he invoked the name [of Avalokiteśvara] without ceasing.

He saw with his own eyes Avalokiteśvara emitting light that shone upon him; his shackles fell off and the gate opened. Following the light, he departed. After traveling twenty li, the radiance finally faded.
The source is the same as above.

During the Long’an era of the Jin dynasty, when the monk Huida was digging for licorice roots on the northern slopes of the mountain, the Qiang people were suffering from famine and were capturing and eating humans.
Huida was captured by them and placed inside a wooden frame; they selected the fattest individuals to eat first. Huida was filled with extreme fear. One—
In his heart he invoked the name of Avalokiteśvara and recited the "Universal Gate" Chapter (*Pumen pin*). The man who had been eating them consumed them all;

only Sengda and the child remained. His life was now but a single day away. Sengda maintained his recitation without ceasing. At dawn, suddenly a tiger leapt out from the brush, its roar shaking the mountains.
The Qiang people fled in terror, but the tiger merely bit at the rafters and departed. Sengda and the child were able to escape.
Exemption. From the *Tiantai Bie xingshu* (Separate Commentary on the Practice).
Furthermore, during the late Qin dynasty, when military conflicts arose like swarms of bees, the rebel forces captured Xu Yi and intended to execute him; they then buried him—
With his two feet bound and his hair tied to a tree, he focused his mind with single-minded devotion upon Avalokiteśvara during the night.
After a short while, he fell asleep. A person in a dream said to him, "The situation is now at its most critical; how can you afford to sleep? Daoyi immediately started up in alarm.

He saw that the guards were all exhausted and fast asleep. Daoyi then exerted himself; once his hands and hair were loosened, his feet were also freed. He walked some hundred paces and hid himself in the grass.
While in the thicket, he heard pursuers approaching with torches arrayed like stars; yet, in the end, no one saw him. At daybreak, the bandits dispersed, and he was thus spared.
This is recorded in the *Shi Fu Zhuan* (Biography of Shi Fu).
Regarding those who seek a son and obtain one:
During the Jin dynasty, there was Sun Daode of Yizhou. He was over fifty years old and had no offspring.
A monk instructed him to recite the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* with a sincere heart, and he followed this advice immediately. Within a few days, his wife herself had a dream.
She immediately became pregnant and subsequently gave birth to a son. This is recorded in the *Xie Fu Zhuan*.

Regarding the manifestation of the body and the preaching of the Dharma during the Dahe era of the Tang dynasty: Emperor Wenzong was fond of clams. Previously, officials along the coastal regions had taken turns presenting them to him, which caused great hardship for the people.

One day, among the food served at his meal, there was a piece that had been split but did not spring back together. The Emperor, considering this a marvel, immediately burned incense and offered prayers to it.
Suddenly, it transformed into the form of a Bodhisattva, fully endowed with the marks of a Brahma.

It was immediately placed within a casket of gold-dusted sandalwood and covered with fine brocade, then bestowed upon Xingshan Monastery so that the assembly of monks might gaze upon and pay homage to it. Thereupon, the Emperor questioned his ministers as to what kind of auspicious omen this was.

Some replied, "At Mount Daxi there is the Chan Master Weizheng, who has a profound understanding of the Buddha-dharma and possesses vast learning and a powerful memory. The Emperor then commanded him [to go].

He was summoned and questioned about the matter. The Master said, "Your servant has heard that no phenomenon occurs without a corresponding cause; this is merely to inspire Your Majesty’s faith. Thus, a sutra states:
'If there are those who are to be saved by means of this body, he shall manifest this very body and preach the Dharma for them.
" The Emperor said, "The Bodhisattva’s body has indeed appeared, yet we have not yet heard him preach the Dharma. The Master replied, "Your Majesty beholds this as..."
"Is it permanent or impermanent? Is it faith or lack of faith? The Emperor said, "This is a most marvelous matter; I believe it with deep conviction.
The Master said, "Your Majesty has already heard the teaching of the Dharma. At that time, the Emperor’s heart was filled with joy, having attained what he had never experienced before.

He issued an edict for all monasteries throughout the realm to establish statues of Avalokiteśvara in order to repay this extraordinary grace. [The Master] spoke privately, saying: "The Bodhisattva uses his own body as a tongue..."
It is said that Emperor Wenzong listened with his mind as his ear.

[The story of] Xian appearing in the body of a young girl and the wife of Malang is unknown as to its origins. Although the Buddhist teachings flourished during the Great Tang, the local customs in the region west of the Pass favored horsemanship and archery.

She had never even heard the names of the Triple Gem. Her wife, pitying her ignorance, went to her home. When people saw the young girl’s refined bearing, they wished to adopt her as their own daughter.
The girl said, "I have no parents and I too wish to have a home. However, I do not desire worldly wealth;
I only wish to serve one who is intelligent, virtuous, and capable of reciting the Buddhist scriptures. The men all gathered together.
[The Master] observed this. The woman then gave him the "Universal Gate Chapter" (*Pumenpin*), saying, "If you can master this in a single night, I shall return to you.
By the following day, more than twenty people had finished reciting it. The woman said, "I am but a single woman whose family lineage has been pure for generations;
I cannot serve many men with one body. You may recite another. She then gave him the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. By dawn, he had mastered it.
The number ten. The girl further bestowed upon him seven fascicles of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and instructed him to master them within three days.
When the time arrived, only the son of the Ma family was able to penetrate them thoroughly. The girl said, "Since you have surpassed all others, you may inform your parents;

once the marriage gifts for the betrothal have been prepared, we shall then formalize the union. Thereupon, the Ma family welcomed her with due ceremony. As she was about to enter the gate, she spoke again, saying: "Just now..."
The hostess’s body was small and frail; she felt unwell and requested a separate room, saying, "I shall wait for peace before meeting you.
Consequently, she stayed in another chamber. Before the guests had even dispersed, the woman passed away and her body began to decay. She was then buried, but not many days later—
There was a monk wearing a purple *kāṣāya*, whose appearance was ancient and austere. He came seeking the woman, and the Ma family led him to the burial site.
The monk then used his mendicant’s staff to part the sand and soil, revealing that the corpse had already decomposed; only the golden chain remained upon the bones.
The monk took it and washed it in the river, then suspended it upon his staff and said to the assembly: "This holy one pities you all for your lack of faith in the True Dharma."

She preached the Dharma and used skillful means to instruct and transform them, urging them to contemplate the causes of goodness so as to avoid falling into the sea of suffering. Suddenly, she ascended into the air and departed.

When the multitude saw this, they wept with grief and paid homage to her incessantly. From that time on, the entire region venerated the Buddha and recited the sutras; this was due to the power of the woman.
The Valley and Mountain Wayfarer’s Praise of Avalokiteśvara says:
"If you wish to see Avalokiteśvara truly, [look at] the horse-herding girl on the sands of the Jinshe River.
Chan Master Ti of Wanshou in Pingjiang composed this verse:
Extremely beautiful, whose daughter is she? A hundred times more intelligent than Ma Lang.
It is laughable that by the banks of the Jinshe Sands they made an appointment; from beginning to end, their union was not destined to be a pair.
She manifests in the body of a bhikṣuṇī.
The Silla National Preceptor Gyeongheung resided at Samnangsa Temple in the capital. Having been ill for a long time without recovery, a nun requested an audience; a gatekeeper led him to see her.
The nun said, "Although you, Master, have realized the Great Dharma, you have formed a body from the four great elements;
how could you be free from illness? There are four kinds of illnesses that arise from these four great elements. The first is physical illness, primarily caused by wind, phlegm, heat, and bile."

The second is the disease of the mind, characterized primarily by insanity and delusion. The third is the disease of external factors, characterized primarily by injuries from blades or staves and excessive physical exertion.
The fourth is the disease of combined causes, characterized primarily by hunger, thirst, cold, heat, suffering, pleasure, sorrow, and joy.
Other categories arise through mutual interdependence; when one major factor is disturbed, a hundred diseases arise together. Now, the Master’s illness is not [of these kinds].
It is appropriate to regard medical treatment as a form of play. Thereupon, he fashioned eleven masks and danced with them.
The Master watched their strange and wondrous expressions and was quite pleased; he did not realize that his illness had departed. When the nun emerged, the Master sent someone to follow her.
She entered the Buddha hall of Nanhua Temple and hid there, holding her bamboo staff while standing before the Eleven-faced [Avalokiteśvara].
Before the Avalokiteśvara Image. From the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Eastern Sea*, Volume Five.
Section Fifteen: Chapter on Dhāraṇīs; Chapter on King Subhavyūha; Chapter on Samantabhadra’s Exhortation.
As Chong emerged from the crevice, the ghost bowed its head;
King Yama pointed him out and sent him to the Fourth Heaven, where a Bodhisattva arrived riding upon a six-tusked elephant,
and Chong emerged from the crevice once more.

During the Jianchu era of the Song dynasty, there was a monk named Puming who left home to become a monk in his youth. By nature he was pure and simple; he constantly maintained a vegetarian diet and wore plain cloth garments.
He made the *Lotus Sūtra* his daily practice, and when reciting it, he used a separate robe and a separate seat, never mixing them with others.

Whenever he reached the "Exhortation" chapter (*Kuanfa pin*), he would see Samantabhadra standing before him riding an elephant. A local man, Wang Daozhen, whose wife was at the point of death, invited the Master.
While he was reciting mantras, just as he was about to enter the gate, the patient fell into a swoon. Suddenly, an object resembling a wild cat, several feet long, emerged from the dog-hole;

at that moment, the patient’s illness was immediately cured. Furthermore, once while he was walking by the water’s edge, a shaman said, "When the divine spirit sees Master Ming, it flees in all directions. (From *Hongzan* 6 and *Xianyingshu*).
The spirit then struck its head in submission.
Baotong cultivated the Brahma-faring with great diligence and constantly recited the *Dhāraṇī Chapter* of the *Lotus Sūtra*, whereby he occasionally manifested supernatural efficacy.

At that time, there was a household of the Zhao family in Yangqiao Village whose wife had been possessed by a spirit; they requested Baotong to perform incantations for her. Once Baotong arrived, the spirit immediately...
He manifested his form and issued a public proclamation, saying: "A deity resides within this village; it is only fitting that you promote its welfare.

Why, then, do you instead possess people? The deity replied, "This is not the disciple's doing; these are merely minor spirits under my command. He then summoned the minor spirits before him and rebuked them.
Because of this, Zhao’s wife recovered. However, her illness later recurred; she sang and wailed all day long and came again to report the matter to Tong.
When Tong arrived once more, he saw the ghost he had reprimanded standing before the sickbed. Tong said, "I previously warned you to depart; why have you come back?
If you do not leave, I shall recite a mantra to cause your head to split into seven pieces, like an arjaka flower."
It was a branch of a pear tree. The ghost then bowed its head and begged for mercy; there was no need for incantations. From then on, his illness was cured, and the ghost never returned again.

This account of events from the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty is found in the *Lingrui ji* (Collection of Auspicious Omens) and the seventh fascicle of the *Hongzan xianying lu* (Extensive Praise of Manifested Responses).
King Yama pointed out Shi Daojin of the Fourth Heaven.
Daojin was a native of Jingzhou. He recited this scripture and lived on a single meal a day in simple robes, possessing a capacity almost equal to that of a man who has encountered the Dharma.

While residing at Biancai Temple, he suddenly collapsed and his breath grew faint. After several days, he saw himself being summoned and recorded by an official of the underworld. As he was about to be led away—
He arrived before the King. The King said, "Master, you have recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and your observance of the precepts has been pure; you ought to have been reborn in the fourth heaven.
As a disciple of the World-Honored One Maitreya, I fear that this body of mine, burdened by evil, will not meet you again. Therefore, I wished to see you; I pray that you will grant me salvation.
Thereupon, Huixin briefly regained consciousness and related everything in detail to the monks. Having finished speaking, he passed away. (From *Hongzan*).

8. When the Bodhisattva arrived riding a six-tusked elephant, there was a monk whose name has been lost, who was at Donglin in Lingyan Temple reciting the Lotus Sūtra with great diligence. Every time...
With utmost sincerity, he entered [the cave]. He purified himself inside and burned incense to worship the Buddha, seeking a sign of verification.

At first, a large snake and a pheasant-deer both came and stood there listening. Once the recitation was finished, they dispersed. At midday, the mountain deity brought food and came personally to make offerings.
Later, he suddenly saw a radiance descend from the eastern mountain. A great Bodhisattva, riding upon a six-tusked white elephant and surrounded by a vast assembly, appeared directly before him.
The monk prostrated toward the light, his joy reaching its deepest extent. All his doubts and textual omissions were fully explained and resolved for him.
The rest of the assembly merely smelled a wondrous fragrance, which only faded after a long time. (Recorded in *Hongzan*, fascicle 7.)
In the sixteenth section:
A young nun recites the True Explanations; a maidservant attains spiritual communion with the Brahma realm;
boatmen are protected as they cross over; and celestial music comes to welcome them.
I deeply revere the mountain man’s mastery of calligraphy, which is worthy of being sung as a celebration of Master Cuimok’s auspicious assembly;
light issues from the corners of his mouth and lotus blossoms grow from the root of his tongue.
Whether lecturing or questioning, the disciples of Boryam appear, while at Lotus Flower Monastery, they seem to read and expound.

Rare birds appeared as auspicious omens; my deceased younger sister manifested signs of her awakening. Her tongue remained intact after being burned, and she recited the scriptures without alteration—not a single character was changed.
From her fingernails grew five-colored flowers, and this young nun brought forth the true essence of the teachings through her recitation.
The daughter of Jiang Mi, a University Doctor of the Liang dynasty, entered the monastic life at a young age and was named Sengfa.

When she was eight or nine years old, she would sometimes sit in quiet meditation with her eyes closed and recite a fascicle of the Lotus Sūtra. The monastics and laypeople of Yangzhou all acclaimed this as being divinely bestowed.
Fei Changfang said: "As verified by the sūtras and śāstras, this principle is perfectly clear. This arises from past habituation and is not a divine revelation bestowed upon opening the spirit;
it is a matter of a previous life, remembered and not forgotten—how marvelous is its spiritual efficacy! (From *Hongzan*, fascicle 2).

The female attendants were mysteriously attuned to the Brahma realm, and their conduct was particularly solemn. Cui Yiqi had a Turkic servant girl who was originally illiterate. During the Linde era, she died of illness;
